body_md:
\label{lem:ladder-ramsey}
For every $r\ge3$ and $m\ge2$, there is an integer $M\ge m$ such that every rainbow $r$-palette $P$ whose underlying $r$-graph contains an $M$-ladder admits a homomorphism $S_m^{p,q}\to P$ for some distinct $p,q\in[r]$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $M\coloneqq R_2(m;r!)$, where $R_2(m;r!)$ is the $r!$-color Ramsey number for pairs. Fix an $M$-ladder in $H(P)$ with spine vertices $b_1,\ldots,b_M$ and cores $A_1,\ldots,A_{M-1}$, and order each core arbitrarily. For each $i<j$, choose an admissible permutation of $A_i\cup\{b_i,b_j\}$. Color the pair $\{i,j\}$ by the positions of $b_i$, $b_j$, and the ordered core vertices in this tuple. There are at most $r!$ colors, so Ramsey's theorem gives a homogeneous set of $m$ indices.

On this set, the earlier and later spine vertices occupy fixed positions $p\ne q$, and each ordered core vertex also occupies a fixed position. Map the spine vertices of $S_m^{p,q}$ to the selected spine vertices in increasing order, and map each $c_{i,\ell}$ to the vertex in the corresponding core occupying position $\ell$. Homogeneity makes this choice independent of the later spine vertex, so the map takes every tuple of $S_m^{p,q}$ to an admissible tuple of $P$. This gives the required homomorphism, which may identify auxiliary colors when different cores intersect.

label: lem:ladder-coloring

body_md:
\label{lem:ladder-coloring}
The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}[beginpenalty=10000]
\item We have $\lambda(R_{p,q})=4r^{-r}$.
\item For every $m\ge2$, we have $\lambda(S_m^{p,q})=r^{-r}$.
\item We have $\operatorname{Col}(R_{p,q})=\bigcup_{m=2}^{\infty}\operatorname{Col}(S_m^{p,q})$. More precisely, for every $m\ge2$, each $R_{p,q}$-colorable $r$-graph with at most $m$ vertices is $S_m^{p,q}$-colorable.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), the polynomial of $R_{p,q}$ is the single monomial $x_a^2\prod_{\ell\in[r]\setminus\{p,q\}}x_{z_\ell}$. Its maximum is attained at $x_a=2/r$ and $x_{z_\ell}=1/r$, giving $\lambda(R_{p,q})=4r^{-r}$.

For (ii), write $x_i$ for the weight of $b_i$, $y_{i,\ell}$ for that of $c_{i,\ell}$, and put $B\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[m]}x_i$ and $Y_\ell\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[m-1]}y_{i,\ell}$. It follows from the definition of $S_m^{p,q}$ that
\[
\Lambda_{S_m^{p,q}}
=\sum_{i\in[m-1]}x_i\left(\sum_{j=i+1}^m x_j\right)\prod_{\ell\in[r]\setminus\{p,q\}}y_{i,\ell}
\le\frac{B^2}{4}\prod_{\ell\in[r]\setminus\{p,q\}}Y_\ell
\le r^{-r}.
\]
For the first inequality, use $x_i\sum_{j=i+1}^m x_j\le B^2/4$ and $\sum_{i\in[m-1]}\prod_{\ell\in[r]\setminus\{p,q\}}y_{i,\ell}\le\prod_{\ell\in[r]\setminus\{p,q\}}Y_\ell$. The last inequality follows by applying AM--GM to $B/2,B/2$ and the $r-2$ numbers $Y_\ell$. Assigning weight $1/r$ to each color of one admissible tuple gives equality.

For (iii), the map $b_i\mapsto a$, $c_{i,\ell}\mapsto z_\ell$ gives a homomorphism $S_m^{p,q}\to R_{p,q}$. To prove the reverse inclusion, fix an $R_{p,q}$-coloring of an $r$-graph with ordered vertices $1,\ldots,N$. The conclusion is immediate for an edgeless $r$-graph, so assume $N\ge r$. For an $(r-1)$-face $T$, write $T[h]$ for its $h$th vertex. Define
\[
h_\ell\coloneqq\begin{cases}q-1,&\text{if }\ell<q,\\q,&\text{if }\ell>q,\end{cases}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\sigma(v)\coloneqq\begin{cases}N+1-v,&\text{if }p<q,\\v,&\text{if }p>q.\end{cases}
\]
Here $h_\ell$ is defined for every $\ell\in[r]\setminus\{q\}$ and belongs to $[r-1]$. Recolor each $(r-1)$-face contained in an edge according to $a\mapsto b_{\sigma(T[h_p])}$ and $z_\ell\mapsto c_{\sigma(T[h_\ell]),\ell}$. Consider an edge $v_1<\cdots<v_r$. The faces in position $p$ and in every position $\ell\ne p,q$ all select $v_q$. They therefore receive the same first index $i\coloneqq \sigma(v_q)$. The face in position $q$ selects $v_{q-1}$ if $p<q$ and $v_{q+1}$ if $p>q$. Its index $j$ satisfies $i<j$ in both cases. The resulting tuple belongs to $S_N^{p,q}$. The color assigned to a face depends only on that face, so the rule is consistent on shared faces. Unused faces can be colored arbitrarily. Finally $S_N^{p,q}$ maps to $S_m^{p,q}$ when $N\le m$.

title: Proof

\[
\mathcal F_0\coloneqq\{F_{p,q}\colon 1\le p<q\le r\}.

Write $F_{q,p}\coloneqq F_{p,q}$ when the positions are listed in the opposite order. Put $m\coloneqq\max\{2,|V(F_{p,q})|\colon p<q\}$ and let $M$ be given by \cref{lem:ladder-ramsey} for these $r$ and $m$.

If an admissible tuple of $P$ repeats a color in positions $p,q$, there is a homomorphism $R_{p,q}\to P$; the other colors of $R_{p,q}$ may also be identified. Thus $F_{p,q}$ would be $P$-colorable, contradicting the deficiency of $P$. This excludes all repeated-color tuples.

It remains to exclude an $M$-ladder. If $P$ contains an $M$-ladder, then \cref{lem:ladder-ramsey} gives $S_m^{p,q}\to P$ for some distinct $p,q\in[r]$. By \cref{lem:ladder-coloring}(iii), $F_{p,q}$ is $S_m^{p,q}$-colorable and hence $P$-colorable, a contradiction.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $t=0$, then $\lambda(P_n)<r^{-r}$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Since every nonempty finite $r$-palette has Lagrangian at least $r^{-r}$ by \cref{lem:finite-values}, we have $P_n=\varnothing$ for all such $n$, and a one-color palette with no admissible tuple suffices. Assume $t>0$ and discard finitely many terms so that $\lambda(P_n)>0$ for every $n$.

To justify the derivative calculations for countable palettes, we first establish convergence and continuity of the defining series.
For a countable palette $P$, the tuple sum defining $\Lambda_P$ extends to $\ell^1(C(P))$, the space of real weightings with $\|\boldsymbol x\|_1\coloneqq\sum_{c\in C(P)}|x_c|<\infty$. The series converges absolutely because $\sum_{(c_1,\ldots,c_r)\in P}\prod_{i\in[r]}|x_{c_i}|\le\|\boldsymbol x\|_1^r$. Expanding a difference of products gives
\[
|\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)-\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol y)|
\le r\max\{\|\boldsymbol x\|_1,\|\boldsymbol y\|_1\}^{r-1}\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol y\|_1.
\]

If $P$ is rainbow, its first and second derivatives are obtained by differentiating the monomials in~\eqref{eq:sym-polynomial} term by term. For distinct colors $u,v$ and every $\boldsymbol x\in\ell^1(C(P))$, the resulting series satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\partial_u\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)|
&\le\sum_{\substack{e\in H(P)\\u\in e}}m_e\prod_{w\in e\setminus\{u\}}|x_w|
\le r\|\boldsymbol x\|_1^{r-1},\\
|\partial_u\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)|
&\le\sum_{\substack{e\in H(P)\\u,v\in e}}m_e\prod_{w\in e\setminus\{u,v\}}|x_w|
\le r(r-1)\|\boldsymbol x\|_1^{r-2},
\end{aligned}
\]
and $\partial_u^2\Lambda_P=0$. These bounds follow from $m_e\le r!$ and $\sum_{A\in\binom{C(P)}j}\prod_{w\in A}|x_w|\le\|\boldsymbol x\|_1^j/j!$. Applying the same difference-of-products estimate to the derivative series shows that they depend continuously on $\boldsymbol x$ in the $\ell^1$ norm, uniformly in their coordinate indices. In particular, the sums defining first and second variations along $\ell^1$ directions converge absolutely.

The real separable \emph{Hilbert spaces} used below can be viewed as finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces or as $\ell^2$, the space of real sequences with $\|\boldsymbol{a}\|^2\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_i^2<\infty$ and inner product $\langle\boldsymbol{a},\boldsymbol{b}\rangle\coloneqq\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} a_i b_i$. For finite palettes, finitely many dimensions suffice.

We first represent the entries of the Hessian at an optimal weighting as squared distances between vectors on a sphere. The passage from a quadratic-form inequality to a squared-distance representation follows Schoenberg~\cite{schoenberg}; the argument below also identifies the common radius and the weighted center.

\begin{claim}\label{lem:hessian}
Let $P$ be a finite or countable rainbow $r$-palette. Suppose a probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ has all coordinates positive and attains $\lambda(P)>0$. Let $\mathsf{H}\coloneqq(\mathsf{H}_{uv})\in\mathbb{R}^{C(P)\times C(P)}$ be the Hessian of $\Lambda_P$ at $\boldsymbol x$. There are vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ in a Hilbert space, indexed by $v\in C(P)$, with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[beginpenalty=10000]
\item $\|\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=r(r-1)\lambda(P)/2$ for every $v\in C(P)$.
\item $\mathsf{H}_{uv}=\|\boldsymbol{q}_u-\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2$ for every $u,v\in C(P)$.
\item $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v\boldsymbol{q}_v=0$.
\item If $P$ is finite and $\boldsymbol x$ has minimum support among its optimal weightings, then the $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ are pairwise distinct.
\end{enumerate}
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Put $d\coloneqq r(r-1)\lambda(P)$. Applying the method of Lagrange multipliers to any two coordinates $u,v$, with all other weights fixed, gives $\partial_u\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)$. Since $\Lambda_P$ is homogeneous of degree $r$, Euler's identity gives $\sum_{v\in C(P)} x_v\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r\lambda(P)$. Since the partial derivatives are equal and $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v=1$, the gradient vector satisfies $\nabla\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=(\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x))_{v\in C(P)}=r\lambda(P)\mathbf 1$.

For each color $u$, the first derivative $\partial_u\Lambda_P$ is homogeneous of degree $r-1$. Applying Euler's identity to this function gives $\sum_{v\in C(P)} \mathsf{H}_{uv}x_v=(r-1)\partial_u\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r(r-1)\lambda(P)=d$. Hence $\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol x=d\mathbf 1$. For every finitely supported $\boldsymbol z$ with $\sum_{v\in C(P)}z_v=0$, the weighting $\boldsymbol x+\varepsilon\boldsymbol z$ is feasible for all sufficiently small positive and negative $\varepsilon$, since $\boldsymbol x$ is positive on the support of $\boldsymbol z$. Optimality therefore gives $\left.\frac{d^2}{d\varepsilon^2}\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x+\varepsilon\boldsymbol z)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol z\le0$.

All Hessian entries are bounded by $r!/(r-2)!=r(r-1)$. Finitely supported zero-sum vectors are dense in the zero-sum subspace of $\ell^1$, so the second-order inequality extends to every zero-sum $\ell^1$ vector. The derivative identities above are absolutely convergent.

Since the polynomial is squarefree, we have $\mathsf{H}_{vv}=0$. Set $\mathsf{G}\coloneqq(d\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}-\mathsf{H})/2$. For a finitely supported vector $\boldsymbol z$, write $s\coloneqq\sum_{v\in C(P)}z_v$ and $\boldsymbol y\coloneqq\boldsymbol z-s\boldsymbol x$. The identity $\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol x=d\mathbf 1$ gives
\[
\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{G}\boldsymbol z
=\tfrac12\bigl(ds^2-\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol z\bigr)
=-\tfrac12\boldsymbol y^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol y\ge0.
\]
Thus $\mathsf{G}$ is a positive semidefinite matrix, also when indexed by a countable set. Its Gram representation gives vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ with $\langle \boldsymbol{q}_u,\boldsymbol{q}_v\rangle=\mathsf{G}_{uv}$. Since $\mathsf{G}_{vv}=d/2$, we have $\|\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=d/2$ and $\|\boldsymbol{q}_u-\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=\mathsf{G}_{uu}+\mathsf{G}_{vv}-2\mathsf{G}_{uv}=\mathsf{H}_{uv}$, proving (i) and (ii). Moreover, the vector sum $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v\boldsymbol{q}_v$ converges absolutely and has squared norm $\boldsymbol x^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{G}\boldsymbol x=0$, so it is zero, proving (iii).

For (iv), the weight-transfer argument of Motzkin and Straus~\cite{motzkin-straus} and Frankl and R\"odl~\cite{frankl-rodl} shows that, at an optimal weighting of minimum support on a finite palette, any two colors of positive weight lie in a common underlying edge. Otherwise the polynomial is affine when weight is transferred between those colors, and optimality permits deleting one of them. A common edge, positive weights, and nonnegative coefficients give $\mathsf{H}_{uv}>0$. The distance formula then implies $\boldsymbol{q}_u\ne \boldsymbol{q}_v$.
\end{proof}

For a Borel probability measure $\nu$ on a separable Hilbert space, a point $\boldsymbol{q}$ is an \emph{atom} if $\nu(\{\boldsymbol{q}\})>0$. The set of atoms is at most countable. We call $\nu$ \emph{atomic}, or \emph{purely atomic}, if all its probability lies on these atoms, that is, $\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}\colon\nu(\{\boldsymbol{q}\})>0}\nu(\{\boldsymbol{q}\})=1$. The restriction of $\nu$ to the complement of its atoms is its \emph{nonatomic part}.

To apply \cref{lem:hessian} to each $P_n$, choose an optimal weighting of minimum support and restrict $P_n$ to this support. Denote its positive weights by $x_v^{(n)}$. Put $c_n\coloneqq r(r-1)\lambda(P_n)$ and $c\coloneqq r(r-1)t$, so $\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n=c$. By \cref{lem:hessian}, there are pairwise distinct vectors $\boldsymbol{p}_v^{(n)}$ with $\|\boldsymbol{p}_v^{(n)}\|^2=c_n/2$ and $\mathsf{H}_{uv}^{(n)}=c_n-2\langle \boldsymbol{p}_u^{(n)},\boldsymbol{p}_v^{(n)}\rangle$. Let $\mu_n\coloneqq\sum_{v\in C(P_n)}x_v^{(n)}\delta_{\boldsymbol{p}_v^{(n)}}$ be the probability distribution of these vectors. Here $\delta_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ denotes the probability measure concentrated at $\boldsymbol{q}$.

To control uniformly in $n$ the error from truncating inner products to finitely many coordinates, rotate each configuration so that its weighted second-moment matrix is diagonal. Its $(i,j)$ entry is $\sum_{v\in C(P_n)} x_v^{(n)}p_{v,i}^{(n)}p_{v,j}^{(n)}$. The matrix is real symmetric and positive semidefinite, so the spectral theorem provides an orthogonal change of coordinates that diagonalizes it and preserves all norms and inner products. Order the diagonal entries so that $\rho_{n,1}\ge\rho_{n,2}\ge\cdots\ge0$; their sum is $c_n/2$. Embed all these configurations into $\ell^2$. They lie in a common closed ball centered at the origin. In the coordinatewise topology, this ball is a closed subset of a countable product of compact intervals, since its radius bound can be checked on finite sums of squared coordinates. The ball is therefore compact and metrizable. Passing to a subsequence, $\mu_n$ converges weakly on that ball to a probability measure $\mu$, meaning that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\int\varphi\,\mathrm d\mu_n=\int\varphi\,\mathrm d\mu$ for every bounded continuous real-valued function $\varphi$ on the ball with its coordinatewise topology. The Skorokhod representation theorem~\cite{billingsley} gives random vectors $\boldsymbol{p}_n$ and $\boldsymbol{p}$, with distributions $\mu_n$ and $\mu$, on $([0,1],\mathrm{Leb})$ such that, for almost every $s$, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}p_{n,j}(s)=p_j(s)$ for every $j\ge1$. Here $\mathrm{Leb}$ denotes Lebesgue measure, and for measurable subsets of $[0,1]^k$ we write $|\cdot|$ for their Lebesgue measure. For almost every $s$ and every positive integer $L$, coordinatewise convergence gives
\[
\sum_{j=1}^L p_j(s)^2
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^L p_{n,j}(s)^2
\le\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{c_n}{2}
=\frac c2.
\]
Letting $L$ tend to infinity shows that $\|\boldsymbol{p}(s)\|^2\le c/2$ almost everywhere. Since the finite vectors are pairwise distinct, $\boldsymbol{p}_n(s)$ determines a unique color $\phi_n(s)$ of $P_n$, with distribution $(x_v^{(n)})_v$.

We next show that if $\mu$ has a nonzero nonatomic part or an atom of squared norm less than $c/2$, then one of the finite palettes $P_n$ contains an $M$-ladder. For this purpose, we express the Hessian entries as symmetric kernels and prove their $L^2$ convergence. Define
\[
K_n(s,t)\coloneqq c_n-2\langle \boldsymbol{p}_n(s),\boldsymbol{p}_n(t)\rangle,
\quad\text{and}\quad
K(s,t)\coloneqq c-2\langle \boldsymbol{p}(s),\boldsymbol{p}(t)\rangle.
\]
\begin{claim}\label{clm:kernel-convergence}
The kernels satisfy $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|K_n-K\|_{L^2([0,1]^2)}=0$. That is, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_{[0,1]^2}|K_n(s,t)-K(s,t)|^2\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d t=0$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Put $C_0\coloneqq\sup_{n\ge1}c_n/2<\infty$. For every $n\ge1$ and positive integer $L$, the diagonal entries $\rho_{n,j}$ of the second-moment matrix are nonnegative and nonincreasing, with sum $c_n/2\le C_0$, so $\rho_{n,L+1}\le C_0/(L+1)$. It follows that $\sum_{j=L+1}^{\infty}\rho_{n,j}^2\le\rho_{n,L+1}\sum_{j=L+1}^{\infty}\rho_{n,j}\le C_0^2/(L+1)$.

We now apply this estimate to the error in truncating the inner product. By the diagonalization, $\int_0^1 p_{n,i}(s)p_{n,j}(s)\,\mathrm d s=0$ for $i\ne j$, and $\int_0^1 p_{n,j}(s)^2\,\mathrm d s=\rho_{n,j}$. Expanding the square and integrating therefore gives
\[
\iint_{[0,1]^2}\left|\langle \boldsymbol{p}_n(s),\boldsymbol{p}_n(t)\rangle-
\sum_{j=1}^L p_{n,j}(s)p_{n,j}(t)\right|^2\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d t
=\sum_{j=L+1}^{\infty}\rho_{n,j}^2
\le\frac{C_0^2}{L+1}.
\]
For each fixed $L$, the truncated sums converge in $L^2$ by the almost-everywhere coordinatewise convergence of $\boldsymbol{p}_n$ to $\boldsymbol{p}$ and bounded convergence. To obtain the corresponding tail bound for $\boldsymbol{p}$, note that, for each $j$, bounded convergence gives $\rho_j\coloneqq \int_0^1 p_j(s)^2\,\mathrm d s=\lim_{n\to\infty}\rho_{n,j}$, and, for $i\ne j$, $\int_0^1 p_i(s)p_j(s)\,\mathrm d s=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^1 p_{n,i}(s)p_{n,j}(s)\,\mathrm d s=0$. The sequence $(\rho_j)$ is nonincreasing. Moreover, for every positive integer $L$, $\sum_{j=1}^L\rho_j=\lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=1}^L\rho_{n,j}\le C_0$, so $\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\rho_j\le C_0$. Thus $\sum_{j=L+1}^{\infty}\rho_j^2\le C_0^2/(L+1)$, so the same tail estimate holds for $\boldsymbol{p}$. First choose $L$ large, then let $n$ tend to infinity, which proves the claim.
\end{proof}

In particular, convergence holds in $L^1$. The kernels $K_n$ are nonnegative, being Hessian entries, and $K$ is nonnegative because $\|\boldsymbol{p}(s)\|^2\le c/2$.

Let $m_e^{(n)}$ count the admissible permutations of $e\in H(P_n)$. Define a symmetric function $\omega_n\colon[0,1]^r\to[0,r!]$ by
\[
\omega_n(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\coloneqq
\begin{cases}
m_e^{(n)},&\text{if }e=\{\phi_n(s_1),\ldots,\phi_n(s_r)\}\in H(P_n),\\
0,&\text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $0\le \omega_n\le r!$ and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:f-hessian}
\int_{[0,1]^{r-2}}\omega_n(s,t,u_3,\ldots,u_r)\,\mathrm d u_3\cdots\,\mathrm d u_r
=(r-2)!K_n(s,t).
\end{equation}
The factor $(r-2)!$ counts the orders of the remaining colors of an edge after the first two colors have been fixed; each Hessian monomial occurs once for every such order.

\begin{claim}\label{clm:atomic-limit}
The measure $\mu$ is purely atomic, and every atom has squared norm $c/2$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Let $U\subseteq[0,1]$ be the set of points for which $\boldsymbol{p}(s)$ is not an atom of $\mu$ having squared norm $c/2$. We have $K(s,t)>0$ almost everywhere on $U\times U$. Indeed, $K(s,t)=0$ requires $\boldsymbol{p}(s)=\boldsymbol{p}(t)$ and both vectors to have squared norm $c/2$. The event $K(s,t)=0$ has positive product measure only at an atom with that squared norm, and all such atoms were removed in defining $U$.

Suppose $|U|>0$, and fix $a\in(0,|U|]$. Choose $\gamma>0$ such that $|\{(s,t)\in U^2\colon K(s,t)<\gamma\}|<a^2/2$. For every measurable $S\subseteq U$ with $|S|\ge a$, at least half of $S^2$ lies where $K\ge\gamma$. By \cref{clm:kernel-convergence}, for all sufficiently large $n$,
\[
\int_{S\times S}K_n
\ge\frac{\gamma a^2}{2}-\|K_n-K\|_{L^1}
\ge\frac{\gamma a^2}{4}.
\]
This bound holds uniformly for all such $S$, including sets chosen after $n$.

Since $\omega_n\le r!$, equation~\eqref{eq:f-hessian} gives
\[
\int_{S\times S\times[0,1]^{r-2}}\mathbf1_{\{\omega_n>0\}}
\ge\frac1{r(r-1)}\int_{S\times S}K_n.
\]
If $|S|\ge a$, averaging over $(t,u_3,\ldots,u_r)\in S\times[0,1]^{r-2}$ gives a choice with $\int_S\mathbf1_{\{\omega_n(s,t,u_3,\ldots,u_r)>0\}}\,\mathrm d s\ge\gamma a^2/(4r(r-1))$, since the averaging domain has measure at most 1. Put $b\coloneqq\phi_n(t)$ and $A\coloneqq\{\phi_n(u_3),\ldots,\phi_n(u_r)\}$. Then $S'\coloneqq\{s\in S\colon A\cup\{b,\phi_n(s)\}\in H(P_n)\}$ has measure at least $\gamma a^2/(4r(r-1))$. Positivity ensures that $A$ has $r-2$ distinct colors and is disjoint from $b$.

Starting with $a_0\coloneqq|U|$, make the following choices successively for $0\le i<M-1$. Choose $\gamma_i>0$ as above with $a=a_i$, and then choose $0<a_{i+1}\le\min\{a_i/2,\gamma_i a_i^2/(8r(r-1))\}$. After these finitely many choices, choose a single $n$ for which $\int_{S\times S}K_n\ge\gamma_i a_i^2/4$ holds for every $0\le i<M-1$ and every measurable $S\subseteq U$ with $|S|\ge a_i$. Starting with $S_0\coloneqq U$, repeat the preceding neighborhood selection $M-1$ times to obtain nested sets $S_i$ of measure at least $a_i$, spine vertices $b_i$, and cores $A_i$. Choose $s\in S_{M-1}$ and put $b_M\coloneqq\phi_n(s)$. Every later spine vertex is the color of a point in each earlier selected neighborhood. By the definitions of these neighborhoods, it is distinct from the corresponding earlier spine vertex and from every color in its core. Thus, for every $1\le i<j\le M$, we have $A_i\cap\{b_i,\ldots,b_M\}=\varnothing$ and $A_i\cup\{b_i,b_j\}\in H(P_n)$. This is an $M$-ladder, a contradiction.

Thus $|U|=0$, which proves the claim.
\end{proof}

By \cref{clm:atomic-limit}, write the limit distribution as $\mu=\sum_{i\in I}w_i\delta_{\boldsymbol{p}_i}$, where $I$ is finite or countably infinite, the $\boldsymbol{p}_i$ are distinct with $\|\boldsymbol{p}_i\|^2=c/2$, and the weights satisfy $w_i>0$ and $\sum_{i\in I}w_i=1$.

We now use the atoms as colors while retaining the limiting Lagrangian. Sampling a point from the preimage of each atom under $\boldsymbol{p}$ and taking its color in $P_n$ gives palettes with homomorphisms into $P_n$, and passing to a limit will recover the value $t$.

Let $B_i\coloneqq\{s\colon \boldsymbol{p}(s)=\boldsymbol{p}_i\}$, so $|B_i|=w_i$. Independently for $i\in I$, choose $\xi_i$ according to normalized Lebesgue measure on $B_i$. Define a random palette $Q_n$ on $I$ by declaring $(i_1,\ldots,i_r)$ admissible exactly when $(\phi_n(\xi_{i_1}),\ldots,\phi_n(\xi_{i_r}))\in P_n$. It is therefore rainbow. For every finite $J\subseteq I$, the map $i\mapsto\phi_n(\xi_i)$ is a homomorphism $Q_n[J]\to P_n$. By the observation after \cref{def:ladder}, homomorphisms between rainbow palettes preserve ladders. Thus an $M$-ladder in $Q_n$ would give one in $P_n$, so every $Q_n$ has no $M$-ladder.

Identify a palette on $I$ with the $0/1$ indicators of its admissible tuples, indexed by $I^r$. The resulting space $\{0,1\}^{I^r}$ is compact and metrizable in the product topology. A sequence converges in this topology precisely when the indicator of each fixed tuple eventually agrees with its indicator in the limit. Passing to a subsequence, the laws of $Q_n$ converge weakly to the law of a random palette $Q$.

\begin{claim}\label{clm:sampled-optimum}
Almost surely, $Q$ is rainbow, has no $M$-ladder, and satisfies $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)=\lambda(Q)=t$ for $\boldsymbol w\coloneqq(w_i)_{i\in I}$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Any $M$-ladder is witnessed by finitely many admissible tuples, so it persists under sufficiently small changes in the product topology. Thus the set of palettes containing no $M$-ladder is closed. The rainbow condition is also closed, so weak convergence implies that $Q$ is almost surely rainbow with no $M$-ladder. Fix a nonempty finite $J\subseteq I$ and a palette $R$ on $J$ with $\lambda(R)>t$. If $Q_n[J]=R$, the sampling map gives $R\to P_n$, and hence $\lambda(R)\le\lambda(P_n)$. Since $\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(P_n)=t$, this event is impossible for all sufficiently large $n$. It depends only on the coordinates indexed by $J^r$ and is therefore both open and closed, so weak convergence gives $\mathbb P[Q[J]=R]=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P[Q_n[J]=R]=0$. There are countably many choices of $J$ and $R$, so every finite subpalette of $Q$ has Lagrangian at most $t$ almost surely. By the countable-palette convention, $\lambda(Q)\le t$ almost surely.

We show that the fixed weighting $\boldsymbol w=(w_i)_{i\in I}$ attains $t$ in $Q$. Choose $s_1,\ldots,s_r$ independently and uniformly from $[0,1]$. Since each $\phi_n(s_j)$ has distribution $(x_v^{(n)})_v$, the probability that $(\phi_n(s_1),\ldots,\phi_n(s_r))\in P_n$ is $\lambda(P_n)$. The expectation of $\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)$ is
\[
\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]=\mathbb P\!\left[(\phi_n(s_1),\ldots,\phi_n(s_r))\in P_n\text{ and }\boldsymbol{p}(s_i)\ne\boldsymbol{p}(s_j)\text{ for every }1\le i<j\le r\right].
\]
The second condition says that the points lie in pairwise different sets $B_i$. Indeed, for distinct indices $i_1,\ldots,i_r$, the event $s_j\in B_{i_j}$ for every $j\in[r]$ has probability $w_{i_1}\cdots w_{i_r}$; conditional on this event, the points have the same joint law as $\xi_{i_1},\ldots,\xi_{i_r}$. Terms with repeated indices contribute zero because $Q_n$ is rainbow. Thus $\lambda(P_n)-\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]$ is the probability that the color tuple is admissible and at least 2 sampled points lie in the same $B_i$.

Since $K=0$ on each $B_i\times B_i$ and these sets are pairwise disjoint, we have
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\int_{B_i\times B_i}K_n\le\|K_n-K\|_{L^1}.
\]
By \cref{clm:kernel-convergence}, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|K_n-K\|_{L^1}=0$. Whenever the color tuple is admissible, $\omega_n(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\ge1$. A union bound over pairs of sampled points, followed by the symmetry of $\omega_n$ and~\eqref{eq:f-hessian}, gives
\[
0\le\lambda(P_n)-\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]
\le\binom r2(r-2)!\sum_{i\in I}\int_{B_i\times B_i}K_n.
\]
It follows that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]=t$. To pass to the limiting law, observe that, for fixed $\boldsymbol w$, the value $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)$ depends continuously on the admissible-tuple indicators in the topology of coordinatewise convergence. Indeed, for a nonempty finite set $J\subseteq I$, deleting the tuples that meet $I\setminus J$ while keeping the remaining weights unchanged gives
\[
0\le\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)-\Lambda_{Q[J]}((w_i)_{i\in J})
\le1-\left(\sum_{i\in J}w_i\right)^r
\le r\sum_{i\in I\setminus J}w_i.
\]
The bound is independent of $Q$. As $J$ increases to $I$, the resulting polynomials depend on finitely many tuple indicators and converge uniformly to $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)$, proving continuity. The preceding loss estimate and convergence of laws give $\mathbb E[\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)]=t$. Since $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)\le\lambda(Q)\le t$ almost surely, equality holds almost surely throughout, as required.
\end{proof}

It remains to show that a finite subpalette attains the same Lagrangian as the countable palette.

\begin{claim}\label{lem:countable-compression}
Let $P$ be a countable rainbow palette with no $M$-ladder for some integer $M\ge2$. If a probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ attains a positive value $\lambda(P)$, then a finite subpalette of $P$ has Lagrangian $\lambda(P)$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Discard zero-weight colors and apply \cref{lem:hessian} to $P$ with its optimal weighting $\boldsymbol x$, writing $d\coloneqq r(r-1)\lambda(P)$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ for the resulting vectors. Their common norm is $\sqrt{d/2}$. Suppose first that the vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ take infinitely many distinct values. Choose colors $b_1,b_2,\ldots$ with pairwise distinct vectors. Their boundedness allows passage to a subsequence along which $\boldsymbol{q}_{b_n}$ converges weakly to $\boldsymbol{q}_*$, meaning that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle\boldsymbol{q}_{b_n},\boldsymbol z\rangle=\langle\boldsymbol{q}_*,\boldsymbol z\rangle$ for every vector $\boldsymbol z$ in the Hilbert space. For each $(r-1)$-set $K$ of colors, set $m_{K\cup\{b_n\}}\coloneqq0$ when $b_n\in K$. There are only countably many such sets $K$, and each coefficient takes values in $\{0,1,\ldots,r!\}$. A diagonal argument therefore gives a further subsequence along which, for every fixed $K$, the coefficient $m_{K\cup\{b_n\}}$ is constant for all sufficiently large $n$.

For a fixed color $v$, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}=d-2\langle \boldsymbol{q}_*,\boldsymbol{q}_v\rangle$.
The right side is nonnegative. It is zero only if $\|\boldsymbol{q}_*\|=\sqrt{d/2}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_v=\boldsymbol{q}_*$. Hence it is positive for all but at most one of the selected colors $b_i$.

Expanding the Hessian entry gives
\[
\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v,b_n\}\\|A|=r-2}}
 m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\prod_{w\in A}x_w.
\]
For all sufficiently large $n$, we have $b_n\ne v$. Using the zero-coefficient convention above, we may take the sum over the fixed family of $(r-2)$-sets $A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v\}$. For each such $A$, the preceding diagonal choice with $K=A\cup\{v\}$ makes $m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}$ eventually constant. Since $0\le m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\le r!$ and $\sum_{A\in\binom{C(P)}{r-2}}\prod_{w\in A}x_w\le1/(r-2)!$, the dominated convergence theorem for series gives
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}
=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v\}\\|A|=r-2}}
\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\right)\prod_{w\in A}x_w.
\]
If $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}>0$, at least one summand on the right is positive. Its core $A$ therefore satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty}m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\ge1$. Since this coefficient is eventually constant, we have $A\cup\{v,b_n\}\in H(P)$ for every sufficiently large $n$.

We now select indices $n_1<\cdots<n_M$, avoiding the possible single color with zero Hessian limit. After choosing $b_{n_i}$ for $i<M$, choose a core $A_i$ by the preceding argument with $v=b_{n_i}$. Then choose $n_{i+1}>n_i$ so large that $b_{n_{i+1}}\notin\bigcup_{j=1}^i A_j$ and $A_j\cup\{b_{n_j},b_{n_{i+1}}\}\in H(P)$ for every $j\in[i]$, again avoiding the exceptional color. These choices give $A_i\cap\{b_{n_i},\ldots,b_{n_M}\}=\varnothing$ for every $i\in[M-1]$, and every $A_i\cup\{b_{n_i},b_{n_j}\}$ with $i<j$ is an edge. Thus the selected spine vertices and cores form an $M$-ladder, a contradiction.

The vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ thus take only finitely many distinct values. Partition the colors according to those values. If $u,v$ belong to one part, then $\mathsf{H}_{uv}=0$. Since all weights are positive and all coefficients are nonnegative, no underlying edge contains both colors. The polynomial is therefore affine in the weights of any one part when the weights in the other parts are fixed. At the current optimal weighting, the coefficients of $x_v$ in this affine function are the partial derivatives $\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)$, which are equal for all colors $v$ in that part by the two-coordinate first-order condition. Concentrating the total weight of that part on one color leaves the value unchanged. The resulting weighting is still optimal, so the same argument applies successively to all the other parts. Since there are only finitely many parts, we obtain a finitely supported probability weighting attaining $\lambda(P)$.
\end{proof}

By \cref{clm:sampled-optimum,lem:countable-compression}, a finite subpalette of $Q$ has Lagrangian $t$ almost surely.

To obtain a fixed finite palette, note that there are countably many finite subsets $J\subseteq I$ and only finitely many palettes on each. Hence some fixed finite $J$ and some fixed palette $P$ on $J$ satisfy $\mathbb P[Q[J]=P]>0$ and $\lambda(P)=t$. The event $Q[J]=P$ depends only on the finitely many coordinates indexed by $J^r$, so it is both open and closed in the product topology. Weak convergence therefore gives $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb P[Q_n[J]=P]=\mathbb P[Q[J]=P]>0$. For every sufficiently large $n$ along the chosen subsequence there is therefore a realization with $Q_n[J]=P$. The homomorphism $i\mapsto\phi_n(\xi_i)$ then gives $P\to P_n$. Composing with the inclusions into the original palettes, before restriction to the supports of the chosen optimal weightings, proves the statement of the theorem.

\label{lem:hessian}
Let $P$ be a finite or countable rainbow $r$-palette. Suppose a probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ has all coordinates positive and attains $\lambda(P)>0$. Let $\mathsf{H}\coloneqq(\mathsf{H}_{uv})\in\mathbb{R}^{C(P)\times C(P)}$ be the Hessian of $\Lambda_P$ at $\boldsymbol x$. There are vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ in a Hilbert space, indexed by $v\in C(P)$, with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[beginpenalty=10000]
\item $\|\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=r(r-1)\lambda(P)/2$ for every $v\in C(P)$.
\item $\mathsf{H}_{uv}=\|\boldsymbol{q}_u-\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2$ for every $u,v\in C(P)$.
\item $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v\boldsymbol{q}_v=0$.
\item If $P$ is finite and $\boldsymbol x$ has minimum support among its optimal weightings, then the $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ are pairwise distinct.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $d\coloneqq r(r-1)\lambda(P)$. Applying the method of Lagrange multipliers to any two coordinates $u,v$, with all other weights fixed, gives $\partial_u\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)$. Since $\Lambda_P$ is homogeneous of degree $r$, Euler's identity gives $\sum_{v\in C(P)} x_v\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r\lambda(P)$. Since the partial derivatives are equal and $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v=1$, the gradient vector satisfies $\nabla\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=(\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x))_{v\in C(P)}=r\lambda(P)\mathbf 1$.

For each color $u$, the first derivative $\partial_u\Lambda_P$ is homogeneous of degree $r-1$. Applying Euler's identity to this function gives $\sum_{v\in C(P)} \mathsf{H}_{uv}x_v=(r-1)\partial_u\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)=r(r-1)\lambda(P)=d$. Hence $\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol x=d\mathbf 1$. For every finitely supported $\boldsymbol z$ with $\sum_{v\in C(P)}z_v=0$, the weighting $\boldsymbol x+\varepsilon\boldsymbol z$ is feasible for all sufficiently small positive and negative $\varepsilon$, since $\boldsymbol x$ is positive on the support of $\boldsymbol z$. Optimality therefore gives $\left.\frac{d^2}{d\varepsilon^2}\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x+\varepsilon\boldsymbol z)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}=\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol z\le0$.

All Hessian entries are bounded by $r!/(r-2)!=r(r-1)$. Finitely supported zero-sum vectors are dense in the zero-sum subspace of $\ell^1$, so the second-order inequality extends to every zero-sum $\ell^1$ vector. The derivative identities above are absolutely convergent.

Since the polynomial is squarefree, we have $\mathsf{H}_{vv}=0$. Set $\mathsf{G}\coloneqq(d\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}-\mathsf{H})/2$. For a finitely supported vector $\boldsymbol z$, write $s\coloneqq\sum_{v\in C(P)}z_v$ and $\boldsymbol y\coloneqq\boldsymbol z-s\boldsymbol x$. The identity $\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol x=d\mathbf 1$ gives
\[
\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{G}\boldsymbol z
=\tfrac12\bigl(ds^2-\boldsymbol z^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol z\bigr)
=-\tfrac12\boldsymbol y^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{H}\boldsymbol y\ge0.
\]
Thus $\mathsf{G}$ is a positive semidefinite matrix, also when indexed by a countable set. Its Gram representation gives vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ with $\langle \boldsymbol{q}_u,\boldsymbol{q}_v\rangle=\mathsf{G}_{uv}$. Since $\mathsf{G}_{vv}=d/2$, we have $\|\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=d/2$ and $\|\boldsymbol{q}_u-\boldsymbol{q}_v\|^2=\mathsf{G}_{uu}+\mathsf{G}_{vv}-2\mathsf{G}_{uv}=\mathsf{H}_{uv}$, proving (i) and (ii). Moreover, the vector sum $\sum_{v\in C(P)}x_v\boldsymbol{q}_v$ converges absolutely and has squared norm $\boldsymbol x^{\mathsf T}\mathsf{G}\boldsymbol x=0$, so it is zero, proving (iii).

For (iv), the weight-transfer argument of Motzkin and Straus~\cite{motzkin-straus} and Frankl and R\"odl~\cite{frankl-rodl} shows that, at an optimal weighting of minimum support on a finite palette, any two colors of positive weight lie in a common underlying edge. Otherwise the polynomial is affine when weight is transferred between those colors, and optimality permits deleting one of them. A common edge, positive weights, and nonnegative coefficients give $\mathsf{H}_{uv}>0$. The distance formula then implies $\boldsymbol{q}_u\ne \boldsymbol{q}_v$.

Put $C_0\coloneqq\sup_{n\ge1}c_n/2<\infty$. \[

\sum_{j=1}^L p_{n,j}(s)p_{n,j}(t)\right|^2\,\mathrm d s\,\mathrm d t

\le\frac{C_0^2}{L+1}.
\]

Thus $\lambda(P_n)-\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]$ is the probability that the color tuple is admissible and at least 2 sampled points lie in the same $B_i$.

Since $K=0$ on each $B_i\times B_i$ and these sets are pairwise disjoint, we have
\[
\sum_{i\in I}\int_{B_i\times B_i}K_n\le\|K_n-K\|_{L^1}.
\]
By \cref{clm:kernel-convergence}, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\|K_n-K\|_{L^1}=0$. Whenever the color tuple is admissible, $\omega_n(s_1,\ldots,s_r)\ge1$. A union bound over pairs of sampled points, followed by the symmetry of $\omega_n$ and~\eqref{eq:f-hessian}, gives
\[
0\le\lambda(P_n)-\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]
\le\binom r2(r-2)!\sum_{i\in I}\int_{B_i\times B_i}K_n.
\]
It follows that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb E[\Lambda_{Q_n}(\boldsymbol w)]=t$. To pass to the limiting law, observe that, for fixed $\boldsymbol w$, the value $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)$ depends continuously on the admissible-tuple indicators in the topology of coordinatewise convergence. Indeed, for a nonempty finite set $J\subseteq I$, deleting the tuples that meet $I\setminus J$ while keeping the remaining weights unchanged gives
\[
0\le\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)-\Lambda_{Q[J]}((w_i)_{i\in J})
\le1-\left(\sum_{i\in J}w_i\right)^r
\le r\sum_{i\in I\setminus J}w_i.
\]
The bound is independent of $Q$. As $J$ increases to $I$, the resulting polynomials depend on finitely many tuple indicators and converge uniformly to $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)$, proving continuity. The preceding loss estimate and convergence of laws give $\mathbb E[\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)]=t$. Since $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol w)\le\lambda(Q)\le t$ almost surely, equality holds almost surely throughout, as required.

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{lem:countable-compression}
Let $P$ be a countable rainbow palette with no $M$-ladder for some integer $M\ge2$. If a probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ attains a positive value $\lambda(P)$, then a finite subpalette of $P$ has Lagrangian $\lambda(P)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Discard zero-weight colors and apply \cref{lem:hessian} to $P$ with its optimal weighting $\boldsymbol x$, writing $d\coloneqq r(r-1)\lambda(P)$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ for the resulting vectors. Their common norm is $\sqrt{d/2}$. Suppose first that the vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ take infinitely many distinct values. Choose colors $b_1,b_2,\ldots$ with pairwise distinct vectors. Their boundedness allows passage to a subsequence along which $\boldsymbol{q}_{b_n}$ converges weakly to $\boldsymbol{q}_*$, meaning that $\lim_{n\to\infty}\langle\boldsymbol{q}_{b_n},\boldsymbol z\rangle=\langle\boldsymbol{q}_*,\boldsymbol z\rangle$ for every vector $\boldsymbol z$ in the Hilbert space. For each $(r-1)$-set $K$ of colors, set $m_{K\cup\{b_n\}}\coloneqq0$ when $b_n\in K$. There are only countably many such sets $K$, and each coefficient takes values in $\{0,1,\ldots,r!\}$. A diagonal argument therefore gives a further subsequence along which, for every fixed $K$, the coefficient $m_{K\cup\{b_n\}}$ is constant for all sufficiently large $n$.

For a fixed color $v$, we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}=d-2\langle \boldsymbol{q}_*,\boldsymbol{q}_v\rangle$.
The right side is nonnegative. It is zero only if $\|\boldsymbol{q}_*\|=\sqrt{d/2}$ and $\boldsymbol{q}_v=\boldsymbol{q}_*$. Hence it is positive for all but at most one of the selected colors $b_i$.

Expanding the Hessian entry gives
\[
\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v,b_n\}\\|A|=r-2}}
 m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\prod_{w\in A}x_w.
\]
For all sufficiently large $n$, we have $b_n\ne v$. Using the zero-coefficient convention above, we may take the sum over the fixed family of $(r-2)$-sets $A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v\}$. For each such $A$, the preceding diagonal choice with $K=A\cup\{v\}$ makes $m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}$ eventually constant. Since $0\le m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\le r!$ and $\sum_{A\in\binom{C(P)}{r-2}}\prod_{w\in A}x_w\le1/(r-2)!$, the dominated convergence theorem for series gives
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}
=\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq C(P)\setminus\{v\}\\|A|=r-2}}
\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\right)\prod_{w\in A}x_w.
\]
If $\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathsf{H}_{b_nv}>0$, at least one summand on the right is positive. Its core $A$ therefore satisfies $\lim_{n\to\infty}m_{A\cup\{v,b_n\}}\ge1$. Since this coefficient is eventually constant, we have $A\cup\{v,b_n\}\in H(P)$ for every sufficiently large $n$.

We now select indices $n_1<\cdots<n_M$, avoiding the possible single color with zero Hessian limit. After choosing $b_{n_i}$ for $i<M$, choose a core $A_i$ by the preceding argument with $v=b_{n_i}$. Then choose $n_{i+1}>n_i$ so large that $b_{n_{i+1}}\notin\bigcup_{j=1}^i A_j$ and $A_j\cup\{b_{n_j},b_{n_{i+1}}\}\in H(P)$ for every $j\in[i]$, again avoiding the exceptional color. These choices give $A_i\cap\{b_{n_i},\ldots,b_{n_M}\}=\varnothing$ for every $i\in[M-1]$, and every $A_i\cup\{b_{n_i},b_{n_j}\}$ with $i<j$ is an edge. Thus the selected spine vertices and cores form an $M$-ladder, a contradiction.

The vectors $\boldsymbol{q}_v$ thus take only finitely many distinct values. Partition the colors according to those values. If $u,v$ belong to one part, then $\mathsf{H}_{uv}=0$. Since all weights are positive and all coefficients are nonnegative, no underlying edge contains both colors. The polynomial is therefore affine in the weights of any one part when the weights in the other parts are fixed. At the current optimal weighting, the coefficients of $x_v$ in this affine function are the partial derivatives $\partial_v\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol x)$, which are equal for all colors $v$ in that part by the two-coordinate first-order condition. Concentrating the total weight of that part on one color leaves the value unchanged. The resulting weighting is still optimal, so the same argument applies successively to all the other parts. Since there are only finitely many parts, we obtain a finitely supported probability weighting attaining $\lambda(P)$.

For (i), if $\pi_{r-2}(\mathcal F)=0$, use a palette with no admissible tuples. Otherwise, by~\cref{thm:palette-tools}(i), choose finite $\mathcal F$-deficient palettes $P_n$ with $\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(P_n)=\pi_{r-2}(\mathcal F)$. If a member of $\mathcal F$ were $P$-colorable, it would be $P_n$-colorable, a contradiction. Thus $P$ is $\mathcal F$-deficient.

For (ii), \cref{lem:finite-values} gives $\mathcal D_r\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(r)}$. The polynomial description of the densities below $4r^{-r}$ follows from the rainbow-palette discussion in \cref{sec:palettes}.

To prove algebraicity, we use the fact that the maximum of a rational-coefficient polynomial $f$ over $\mathbb{S}_m$ is a real algebraic number. Its value $y$ is specified by
\[
\exists\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb{S}_m\ \bigl(f(\boldsymbol x)=y\ \wedge\ \forall\boldsymbol z\in\mathbb{S}_m\ f(\boldsymbol z)\le y\bigr).
\]
Quantifier elimination over real closed fields~\cite{bpr} describes this singleton by finitely many polynomial sign conditions over $\mathbb Q$. At least one nonzero polynomial in this description must vanish at $y$; otherwise all its sign conditions would remain unchanged in a neighborhood of $y$, contradicting that the set is a singleton. Thus $y$ is algebraic. Countability follows because there are countably many finite palettes.

By \cref{thm:app-fr-realization}, $\mathcal D_r\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm u,\mathrm{fin}}^{(r)}\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(r)}$. Finite attainment makes these inclusions equalities below $4r^{-r}$. The palette with the single tuple $(a,a,c_3,\ldots,c_r)$, where $a,c_3,\ldots,c_r$ are pairwise distinct, has Lagrangian $(2/r)^2(1/r)^{r-2}=4r^{-r}$. title: Proof
body_md:
We first locate continuum many ordinary Tur\'an densities in a short interval. A number $\alpha\in[0,1)$ is an \emph{ordinary non-jump} for $3$-graphs if $(\alpha,\alpha+\varepsilon)\cap\Pi_{3,\infty}\ne\varnothing$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. Frankl and R\"odl~\cite{frankl-rodl} proved that ordinary non-jumps exist in every uniformity at least 3. For $m\ge3$, we have $\lambda(K_m^{(3)})=(m-1)(m-2)/m^2$.

\begin{claim}\label{lem:localized-ordinary}
Let $m\ge3$. If $\alpha$ is an ordinary non-jump and $\alpha<(m-1)(m-2)/m^2$, then $|\Pi_{3,\infty}\cap[(m-1)(m-2)/m^2,(m-2)/(m+1)]|=2^{\aleph_0}$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Pikhurko~\cite[Section 6, proof of Theorem 2]{pikhurko} constructs distinct ordinary densities from infinite subsets of $\mathbb N$. His proof permits any ordinary non-jump $\alpha$ and any $m$ with $\alpha<(m-1)(m-2)/m^2$. It selects finite $3$-graphs $H_i$ whose normalized Lagrangians lie in $(\alpha,(m-1)(m-2)/m^2)$ and decrease sufficiently rapidly to $\alpha$. Each infinite set $A=\{a_1<a_2<\cdots\}\subseteq\mathbb N$ specifies a recursive construction on an $m$-part partition. Add every triple meeting 3 distinct classes, place a blowup of $H_{a_1}$ in the second class, and repeat the construction with $A\setminus\{a_1\}$ in the first class. Condition (29) in that proof specifies the required rate of decrease, and the comparison argument following (30) shows that the resulting ordinary densities $\tau_A$ are pairwise distinct. The transversal triples give $\tau_A\ge(m-1)(m-2)/m^2$.

We prove the additional upper bound $\tau_A\le (m-2)/(m+1)$. For $\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb{S}_m$, let $E_3\coloneqq\sum_{1\le i<j<k\le m}x_ix_jx_k$ and $Q_3\coloneqq\sum_{\substack{i,j\in[m]\\i\ne j}}x_i^2x_j$. For each triple of indices, applying AM--GM to its 6 terms of the form $x_i^2x_j$ gives a sum at least $6x_ix_jx_k$. Summing over triples gives $(m-2)Q_3\ge6E_3$. Since $1-\sum_{i\in[m]} x_i^3=3Q_3+6E_3$, we obtain $6E_3\le \frac{m-2}{m+1}\left(1-\sum_{i\in[m]} x_i^3\right)$. We also have $(m-1)(m-2)/m^2<(m-2)/(m+1)$. Suppose the normalized Lagrangian of the recursive part is at most $(m-2)/(m+1)$. If $x_i$ is the total weight in class $i$, the normalized polynomial of the whole construction is at most
\[
6E_3+\frac{m-2}{m+1}x_1^3+\lambda(H_{a_1})x_2^3
\le6E_3+\frac{m-2}{m+1}\sum_{i\in[m]} x_i^3\le\frac{m-2}{m+1}.
\]
Starting with an edgeless $3$-graph at the final stage of the recursion, induction gives this bound for every finite stage. In particular, every finite $3$-graph $G$ on $N$ vertices obtained from this construction satisfies $6|G|/N^3\le (m-2)/(m+1)$. Pikhurko identifies $\tau_A$ with the limit of the maximum edge densities of these $3$-graphs as $N$ tends to infinity. Since $\lim_{N\to\infty}N^3/(6\binom N3)=1$, we obtain $\tau_A\le(m-2)/(m+1)$. The pairwise distinct values $\tau_A$ prove the claim.
\end{proof}

Liu and Mubayi~\cite[Theorem 1.1]{liumubayi} proved that $4/9$ is an ordinary non-jump. Since $4/9<12/25$, applying \cref{lem:localized-ordinary} with $m=5$ gives $|\Pi_{3,\infty}\cap[12/25,1/2]|=2^{\aleph_0}$.

The set $\mathcal S\coloneqq\frac16(\Pi_{3,\infty}\cap[12/25,1/2])\subseteq[2/25,1/12]$ has cardinality continuum. By ordinary Lagrangian approximation and \cref{lem:orientation-lift}, each point of $\mathcal S$ is the limit of a sequence in $\mathcal D_3$. Since $1/12<4/27$, the sequence eventually lies in $\mathcal D_3\cap[0,4/27]$. Thus $\mathcal S\subseteq\overline{\mathcal D_3\cap[0,4/27]}$. Deleting the countably many algebraic numbers leaves continuum many transcendental points. Every element of $\mathcal D_3\cap[0,4/27]$ is algebraic, so none of these points belongs to $\mathcal D_3\cap[0,4/27]$.

We now lift these limit points to uniformity $r$ and use finite attainment to exclude them from $\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(r)}$. Fix a transcendental point $t\in\mathcal S$ and finite $3$-palettes $P_n$ with $\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(P_n)=t$. For each fixed $r\ge3$, \cref{lem:orientation-lift} gives $\lambda(\operatorname{lift}_r(P_n))=27r^{-r}\lambda(P_n)$, and hence $\lim_{n\to\infty}\lambda(\operatorname{lift}_r(P_n))=27r^{-r}t$. Each term belongs to $\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(r)}$ by \cref{lem:finite-values}, while $27r^{-r}t\in[(54/25)r^{-r},(9/4)r^{-r}]\subseteq(r^{-r},4r^{-r})$. This limit is transcendental because $27r^{-r}$ is a nonzero rational. By \cref{thm:attainment}(ii), it does not belong to $\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(r)}$. Multiplication by $27r^{-r}$ is injective, so the continuum many choices of $t$ prove (iii).

The set $\mathcal D_3\cap[0,4/27]$ is countably infinite, is not discrete, and contains $\sqrt3/18$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
There are only countably many finite palettes up to relabeling. For every $m\ge2$, the palette on $z,b_1,\ldots,b_m$ with tuples $(z,b_i,b_j)$ for $i<j$ has polynomial $x_z\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}x_{b_i}x_{b_j}$. For fixed $x_z$, we have $\sum_{1\le i<j\le m}x_{b_i}x_{b_j}=\frac12((1-x_z)^2-\sum_{i\in[m]}x_{b_i}^2)$. Cauchy--Schwarz therefore shows that the maximum is attained when $x_{b_i}=(1-x_z)/m$ for every $i\in[m]$. Thus its Lagrangian is
\[
\max_{0\le u\le1}\frac12\left(1-\frac1m\right)u(1-u)^2
=\frac2{27}\left(1-\frac1m\right).
\]
These values converge to $2/27$, which is realized by a palette consisting of 2 permutations of one rainbow triple. For an irrational example, select 1 permutation of each of $123,124$ and 2 permutations of each of $134,234$. The polynomial is $x_1x_2(x_3+x_4)+2(x_1+x_2)x_3x_4$. For fixed $t\coloneqq x_3+x_4$, the polynomial is maximized when $x_1=x_2=(1-t)/2$ and $x_3=x_4=t/2$, and its value is $(t-t^3)/4$. Its maximum on $[0,1]$ is $\sqrt3/18<4/27$, attained at $t=1/\sqrt3$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $S\coloneqq A+B+c+d$ for the total auxiliary weight. Put $\rho_A\coloneqq(A+d-c)/2$ and $\rho_B\coloneqq(B+d-c)/2$, and define
\[
E\coloneqq\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2,
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Delta\coloneqq\frac{2S^3}{27}-\Phi_1-\Phi_2.
\]
Here $\Delta$ is the \emph{deficit} of $\Phi_1+\Phi_2$ from its upper bound $2S^3/27$.
Completing the square in each summand of $\Phi_1$ and $\Phi_2$ gives
\[
\Phi_1=\frac{A(S-A)^2}{4}-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2,
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Phi_2=\frac{B(S-B)^2}{4}-\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2.
\]
In particular, if $S>0$, then we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cyclic-variance}
\max\{\Phi_1,\Phi_2\}\le\left(\frac{S}{3}\right)^3,
\qquad E\le\Delta,
\quad\text{and}\quad
\left(A-\frac{S}{3}\right)^2+\left(B-\frac{S}{3}\right)^2\le\frac{12\Delta}{S}.
\end{equation}
Indeed, we have
\[
\frac{S^3}{27}-\frac{A(S-A)^2}{4}
=\frac14\left(A-\frac{S}{3}\right)^2\left(\frac{4S}{3}-A\right).
\]
Since $A\le S$, we have $4S/3-A\ge S/3$. Applying the same identity with $B$ in place of $A$ gives the stated bounds. The bounds $\Phi_i\le(S/3)^3$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ are attained simultaneously at
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cyclic-test}
a_i=b_i=\frac{S}{3n},
\qquad c=\frac S3\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right),\qquad d=\frac S{3n}.
\end{equation}

For each $i\in\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, put $X_i\coloneqq\{A_i,B_i,A_{i+1},B_{i+1}\}$. These 4 colors are distinct since $n\ge2$. Put $h\coloneqq\max\{0,\rho_A,\rho_B\}$. The next claim bounds the individual weights when $\Delta<h^3/28$ and the sum $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i b_i a_{i+1}b_{i+1}$ otherwise.

\begin{claim}\label{lem:cyclic-control}
If $S>0$ and $\Delta<h^3/28$, then $a_i,b_i\in(S/(27n),9S/(4n)]$ for all $i$. If $\Delta\ge h^3/28$, then $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i b_i a_{i+1}b_{i+1}\le\frac{1675}{16}A\Delta$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
For the first assertion, we have $0<h\le S/2$. By~\eqref{eq:cyclic-variance}, $|\rho_A-\rho_B|^2\le6\Delta/S<3h^2/28<h^2/9$, so $2h/3<\rho_A,\rho_B\le h$. We also have $A+B\ge2S/3-\sqrt{24\Delta/S}>S(2/3-\sqrt{3/28})>S/3$. Let $\widehat u_1,\ldots,\widehat u_{2n}$ be the cyclic sequence alternating $a_i/\rho_A$ and $b_i/\rho_B$. Read the subscripts modulo $2n$. This sequence has sum greater than $2/3$, and
\[
K\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[2n]}\widehat u_i(1-\widehat u_{i+1})^2\le\frac{27E}{8h^3}<\frac{27}{224}<\frac18.
\]
Here the two alternating types of summands in $K$ are $a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2/(\rho_A\rho_B^2)$ and $b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2/(\rho_B\rho_A^2)$. Their denominators are at least $(2h/3)^3$, giving the bound in terms of $E$. For any cyclic nonnegative sequence with sum at least $1/2$ and $K<1/8$, every coordinate is at least $1/2$. Otherwise, either all coordinates are below $1/2$, giving $K>\frac14\sum_{i\in[2n]}\widehat u_i\ge1/8$, or a cyclic transition from a coordinate at least $1/2$ to one below $1/2$ contributes more than $1/8$. Using $\widehat u_{i-1}\ge1/2$ in $\widehat u_{i-1}(1-\widehat u_i)^2\le K$ gives $|\widehat u_i-1|\le\sqrt{2K}<1/2$. Thus $h/3<a_i,b_i<3h/2$. Summing and using $S/3<A+B\le S$ yields $S/(9n)<h<3S/(2n)$, which gives the first assertion.

For the second assertion, write $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)\coloneqq(a_i,b_i,a_{i+1},b_{i+1})$ for the consecutive weights of $X_i$. If the last 3 weights are at most $5h/4$, their product with $u_0$ is at most $(125/64)a_i h^3$. Otherwise choose a largest one, say $u_k>5h/4$ for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$. For $k\in\{1,3\}$, the sum $E$ contains $u_{k-1}(u_k-\rho_B)^2$; for $k=2$, it contains $u_1(u_2-\rho_A)^2$. In either case this term is at least $u_{k-1}u_k^2/25$, since $\rho_A,\rho_B\le h<4u_k/5$. If $u_0u_1u_2u_3=0$, the required bound is immediate. Otherwise, the ratio of $u_0u_1u_2u_3$ to $u_{k-1}u_k^2$ is at most $A$. Indeed, for $k=1,2,3$ it is bounded respectively by $u_2,u_0,u_0$. The term $a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2$ can be used only for $X_{i-1}$ or $X_i$, whereas $b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2$ can be used only for $X_i$. Counting each summand of $E$ at most twice therefore gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i b_i a_{i+1}b_{i+1}\le50AE+\frac{125}{64}Ah^3
\le\left(50+\frac{125\cdot28}{64}\right)A\Delta
=\frac{1675}{16}A\Delta.\qedhere
\]
\end{proof}



We next bound the edge polynomials $R_j$, including their first derivatives at the weighting that is constant within each class.

\begin{claim}\label{lem:connectors}
The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item The $\mathcal M_j$ are pairwise edge-disjoint simple $9$-graphs. The $9$-graph $\bigcup_{j=0}^{q-1}\mathcal M_j$ is $9$-partite, and $\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}R_j\le(S/9)^9$.
\item Every $A$-color has degree 5 and every $B$-color degree 4 in each $\mathcal M_j$. At the weighting $a_i=A/n$, $b_i=B/n$, we have $R_j=A^5B^4/n^8$, $\partial_{a_i}R_j=5(A/n)^4(B/n)^4$, and $\partial_{b_i}R_j=4(A/n)^5(B/n)^3$.
\item If $\Delta\ge h^3/28$, then $R_j\le\frac{1675}{1728}A^4B^2\Delta$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
For (i), observe that the 9 indices defining $E_{j,t}$ in~\eqref{eq:connector-edges} are distinct modulo $2n$. For $j=0$ they form 1 block of 9 consecutive positions. For $j>0$ they form 2 blocks of 4 consecutive positions and 1 isolated position. Of the 2 blocks of length 4, exactly 1 starts at an even index. That block starts at $2t$, which determines $t$, and the isolated index $2t+4+18j$ then determines $j$. The inequality $n\ge36(q+1)$ prevents the isolated index from being adjacent to either block in the cyclic order modulo $2n$. This proves simplicity and disjointness, both within and between the families.

Partition the auxiliary colors $v_0,\ldots,v_{2n-1}$ according to their indices modulo 9. Since $18j\equiv0\pmod9$ and $2n$ is divisible by 9, every connecting edge meets each part exactly once. Standard results on the Lagrangians of complete multipartite hypergraphs therefore give $\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}R_j\le(S/9)^9$, completing (i).

For (ii), translation by 2 positions preserves $\mathcal M_j$ and acts transitively on each of the $A$- and $B$-classes, so the degrees are constant within each class. Its $n$ edges contain 5 $A$-colors and 4 $B$-colors each, giving $5n$ and $4n$ incidences, respectively. Dividing by the $n$ colors in each class gives degrees 5 and 4. At the balanced weighting, each of the $n$ edge monomials equals $(A/n)^5(B/n)^4$, yielding the formula for $R_j$. Differentiating with respect to an $A$-color leaves 4 $A$-weights and 4 $B$-weights in each of its 5 incident edges; for a $B$-color, it leaves 5 $A$-weights and 3 $B$-weights in each of its 4 incident edges. This gives the two derivative formulas.

For (iii), $E_{j,t}$ contains $X_t$. The set $E_{j,t}\setminus X_t$ consists of 3 $A$-colors and 2 $B$-colors. Hence
\[
R_j\le\left(\frac{A}{3}\right)^3\left(\frac{B}{2}\right)^2\sum_{t=0}^{n-1} a_t b_t a_{t+1}b_{t+1}
\le\frac{1675}{1728}A^4B^2\Delta.
\]
The second inequality follows from \cref{lem:cyclic-control}.
\end{proof}


AM--GM, \eqref{eq:piece-bounds}, \eqref{eq:cyclic-variance}, and \cref{lem:connectors}(i) give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-add-four}
\Lambda_{\rm base}\le4T\left(\frac{S}{3}\right)^3\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell\le4\cdot12^{-12},
\quad\text{and}\quad
\Lambda_{\rm add}\le4\left(\frac{S}{9}\right)^9\left(\frac{T}{3}\right)^3\le4\cdot12^{-12}.
\end{equation}
For a lower bound, take the test weighting with $t_\ell=T=1/12$, $S=1/4$, the auxiliary weights in~\eqref{eq:cyclic-test}, and an optimal probability weighting of $P$ scaled to total weight $T$. It yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compiler-test}
\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})\ge12^{-12}\bigl(4+\lambda(P)n^{-8}\bigr)>4\cdot12^{-12}.
\end{equation}
Hence both parts of the polynomial are positive at every optimal weighting, as are all $t$-weights and the group totals $S,T$.

Fix an optimal probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ and put $\eta\coloneqq\Lambda_{\rm add}/\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})\in(0,1)$. We first estimate the total weights of the color classes. At an optimal weighting, all positive coordinates have the same partial derivative. Euler's identity and the total weight 1 show that this common value is $12\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})$. Each base monomial contains every $t_\ell$ to exponent 1, whereas additional monomials contain no $t$-variables. Each base monomial has total degree 3 in the auxiliary variables and total degree 1 in the weights of the colors of $P$; for each additional monomial, these total degrees are 9 and 3, respectively. Multiplying the derivative equations by the corresponding weights and summing over each group, with zero coordinates contributing zero, gives $12t_\ell\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})=\Lambda_{\rm base}$, $12S\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})=3\Lambda_{\rm base}+9\Lambda_{\rm add}$, and $12T\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})=\Lambda_{\rm base}+3\Lambda_{\rm add}$. Dividing by $12\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})$ and using the definition of $\eta$, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:compiler-euler}
t_\ell=\frac{1-\eta}{12},\qquad S=\frac{1+2\eta}{4},\qquad T=\frac{1+2\eta}{12}.
\end{equation}
Since $\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})>4\cdot12^{-12}$, equation~\eqref{eq:base-add-four} gives $\eta<12^{12}\Lambda_{\rm add}/4\le12^{12}(S/9)^9(T/3)^3$. Applying AM--GM to 9 copies of $S/9$ and 3 copies of $T/3$ now gives $\eta<(S+T)^{12}=((4+8\eta)/12)^{12}$.
The function $\eta\mapsto((4+8\eta)/12)^{12}-\eta$ is strictly convex, vanishes at 1, and is negative at $10^{-5}$. Convexity makes it negative throughout $[10^{-5},1)$, whereas the preceding inequality requires it to be positive at $\eta$. Since $0<\eta<1$, we obtain $\eta<10^{-5}$.

Keeping the deficit $\Delta$ in the base polynomial gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-retained}
\Lambda_{\rm base}=2T\left(\frac{2S^3}{27}-\Delta\right)\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell\le4\cdot12^{-12}-2T\Delta\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell.
\end{equation}
Since $\Lambda_{\rm base}=(1-\eta)\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})>4\cdot12^{-12}(1-\eta)$, we have $\Delta<2\cdot12^{-12}\eta/(T\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell)$. Equations~\eqref{eq:compiler-euler} and~\eqref{eq:cyclic-variance} imply
\[
S<\frac{3.00006}{12},\qquad T<\frac{1.00002}{12},\qquad \prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell>\frac{0.9999}{12^8},\quad\text{and}\quad\max\{A,B\}<\frac{1.01}{12}.
\]
For the bound on $\max\{A,B\}$, $12^3\Delta<2\cdot10^{-5}/0.9999$ and $\max\{|A-S/3|,|B-S/3|\}\le\sqrt{12\Delta/S}$ suffice.

We now show that $\Delta<h^3/28$. If $\Delta\ge h^3/28$, then \cref{lem:connectors} and $\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}D_j(\boldsymbol z)\le T^3$ give
\[
\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})\le4\cdot12^{-12}-\left(2T\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell-\frac{1675}{1728}A^4B^2T^3\right)\Delta\le4\cdot12^{-12},
\]
since, after multiplication by $12^9$, the coefficient in parentheses is greater than $2\cdot0.9999-(1675/1728)(1.01)^6(1.00002)^3>0.94$. Here we used $T\ge1/12$ from~\eqref{eq:compiler-euler} as well as the preceding bounds. This contradicts~\eqref{eq:compiler-test}. Hence $\Delta<h^3/28$, and \cref{lem:cyclic-control} gives $a_i,b_i\in(1/(108n),7/(12n))$.
Since every connector has 9 vertices and there are $n$ connectors in each family, we have $R_j\le n(7/(12n))^9=(7/12)^9n^{-8}$. Since $\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}D_j(\boldsymbol z)\le T^3$, we also have $\Lambda_{\rm add}=O(n^{-8})$. By~\eqref{eq:base-retained} and~\eqref{eq:compiler-test}, we have $2T\Delta\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell<\Lambda_{\rm add}$. Since $T\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell$ is bounded below by an absolute positive constant, this gives $\Delta=O(n^{-8})$. Also $\eta<12^{12}\Lambda_{\rm add}/4=O(n^{-8})$.
All implicit constants in this proof are absolute; in particular, they are independent of $P$ and $q$.

We next show that the weights are constant within each auxiliary class. Put $\xi_i\coloneqq a_i-A/n$ and $\zeta_i\coloneqq b_i-B/n$, so $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\xi_i=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\zeta_i=0$. Write $V\coloneqq\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\xi_i^2+\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\zeta_i^2$. Keep $A,B,c,d$, the weighting of $P$, and the $t$-weights fixed, and equalize the weights within each auxiliary class. We denote this balanced weighting by $\bar{\boldsymbol x}$.

Since $b_i>1/(108n)$, we have $E\ge(108n)^{-1}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2\ge\frac1{108}(A/n-\rho_A)^2$, where the second inequality is Cauchy--Schwarz. Together with $E\le\Delta$, this gives $|A/n-\rho_A|\le\sqrt{108\Delta}$; the same argument gives $|B/n-\rho_B|\le\sqrt{108\Delta}$. Expanding the square-completion formulas gives
\begin{align*}
\Phi_1(\bar{\boldsymbol x})-\Phi_1(\boldsymbol x)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i\zeta_i^2+2\left(\frac{B}{n}-\rho_B\right)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\xi_i\zeta_i,\\
\text{and}\qquad \Phi_2(\bar{\boldsymbol x})-\Phi_2(\boldsymbol x)
&=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} b_i\xi_{i+1}^2+2\left(\frac{A}{n}-\rho_A\right)\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\zeta_i\xi_{i+1}.
\end{align*}
Cauchy--Schwarz gives $|\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\xi_i\zeta_i|+|\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\zeta_i\xi_{i+1}|\le V$. The two cross terms therefore have sum at least $-2\sqrt{108\Delta}V$. Since $a_i,b_i>1/(108n)$, the sum of the two differences is at least $(1/(108n)-2\sqrt{108\Delta})V$. Using $\Delta=O(n^{-8})$, we obtain a lower bound of $V/(216n)$ for all sufficiently large $n$. Multiplying by $2T\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell$ shows that the base part increases by at least $\frac{TV}{108n}\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell$.

To bound the possible loss in the additional part, we use \cref{lem:connectors}(ii), which states that the partial derivatives of each $R_j$ at the balanced weighting are constant within each auxiliary class. The weight changes sum to zero in each class, so $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\bigl(\partial_{a_i}R_j(\bar{\boldsymbol x})\xi_i+\partial_{b_i}R_j(\bar{\boldsymbol x})\zeta_i\bigr)=0$. Thus the first-order term in the balancing direction vanishes at $\bar{\boldsymbol x}$. Along the segment from the original point to the balanced weighting, each weight $a_i$ or $b_i$ is at most $7/(12n)$. Each color occurs in at most 5 edges of $\mathcal M_j$, with 8 other vertices per edge. For any 2 distinct colors in an edge, that edge contributes the product of the other 7 weights to the corresponding mixed second derivative of $R_j$. Thus every row sum of the Hessian of $R_j$ with respect to $(a_i,b_i)_{i=0}^{n-1}$ is at most $40(7/(12n))^7$. The Hessian is symmetric with nonnegative entries, so this also bounds its operator norm. Expanding at $\bar{\boldsymbol x}$, where the first-order term vanishes, and using $\|\boldsymbol x-\bar{\boldsymbol x}\|_2^2=V$, Taylor's formula gives $|R_j(\boldsymbol x)-R_j(\bar{\boldsymbol x})|\le\frac12\cdot40(7/(12n))^7V=O(n^{-7})V$. Using $\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}D_j\le T^3$ once more, the additional part can decrease by at most $O(n^{-7})V$. Since $T\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell$ is bounded below by an absolute positive constant, this loss is smaller than the gain in the base part for all sufficiently large $n$ whenever $V>0$, contradicting optimality. This proves (i).

It remains to determine the optimized value and its expansion. At the balanced weighting, every edge polynomial $R_j$ equals $A^5B^4/n^8$, so we have
\[
\sum_{j=0}^{q-1}R_jD_j(\boldsymbol z)=\frac{A^5B^4}{n^8}\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol z).
\]
By homogeneity, optimizing over the weights of the colors of $P$ at fixed total $T$ gives
\[
\max_{\substack{z_c\ge0\ (c\in C(P))\\\sum_{c\in C(P)}z_c=T}}\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol z)=T^3\lambda(P).
\]
Substituting the balanced auxiliary weights, define
\[
\Psi_n(x)\coloneqq\max\Biggl\{2TA\left(\frac{B}{n}+c\right)\left(B-\frac{B}{n}+d\right)\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell+2TB\left(\frac{A}{n}+c\right)\left(A-\frac{A}{n}+d\right)\prod_{\ell=1}^8t_\ell+\frac{A^5B^4T^3}{n^8}x\Biggr\},
\]
where the maximum is over $(A,B,c,d,T,t_1,\ldots,t_8)\in\mathbb{S}_{13}$. This is a compact domain. Every maximizing weighting of $\mathcal H_{n,P}$ is constant within each auxiliary class, and every point in this domain can be completed by an optimal weighting of $P$ scaled to total weight $T$. Hence $\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})=\Psi_n(\lambda(P))$.

On every compact interval of values of $x$, the objective is uniformly continuous jointly in $x$ and the feasible weights. Hence $\Psi_n$ is continuous. For $x>0$, the test weighting gives $\Psi_n(x)\ge12^{-12}(4+xn^{-8})>4\cdot12^{-12}$. At any maximizer the coefficient of $x$ must be positive, because the base part is at most $4\cdot12^{-12}$. For $0<x<y$, testing a maximizing weighting for $x$ at the parameter $y$ gives $\Psi_n(y)\ge\Psi_n(x)+\frac{A^5B^4T^3}{n^8}(y-x)>\Psi_n(x)$, proving strict monotonicity.

Finally, \eqref{eq:cyclic-variance} and~\eqref{eq:compiler-euler}, together with $\Delta=O(n^{-8})$ and $\eta=O(n^{-8})$, give $A,B=1/12+O(n^{-4})$ and $T=1/12+O(n^{-8})$. Hence $A^5B^4T^3=12^{-12}+O(n^{-4})$. Since the base part is at most $4\cdot12^{-12}$ and $\lambda(P)\le1$, we obtain $\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})\le12^{-12}(4+\lambda(P)n^{-8})+O(n^{-12})$. The test weighting in~\eqref{eq:compiler-test} gives the reverse bound $\lambda(\mathcal H_{n,P})\ge12^{-12}(4+\lambda(P)n^{-8})$, proving both the expansion and the nonnegativity of its error in (iii).

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{lem:cyclic-control}
If $S>0$ and $\Delta<h^3/28$, then $a_i,b_i\in(S/(27n),9S/(4n)]$ for all $i$. If $\Delta\ge h^3/28$, then $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i b_i a_{i+1}b_{i+1}\le\frac{1675}{16}A\Delta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the first assertion, we have $0<h\le S/2$. By~\eqref{eq:cyclic-variance}, $|\rho_A-\rho_B|^2\le6\Delta/S<3h^2/28<h^2/9$, so $2h/3<\rho_A,\rho_B\le h$. We also have $A+B\ge2S/3-\sqrt{24\Delta/S}>S(2/3-\sqrt{3/28})>S/3$. Let $\widehat u_1,\ldots,\widehat u_{2n}$ be the cyclic sequence alternating $a_i/\rho_A$ and $b_i/\rho_B$. Read the subscripts modulo $2n$. This sequence has sum greater than $2/3$, and
\[
K\coloneqq\sum_{i\in[2n]}\widehat u_i(1-\widehat u_{i+1})^2\le\frac{27E}{8h^3}<\frac{27}{224}<\frac18.
\]
Here the two alternating types of summands in $K$ are $a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2/(\rho_A\rho_B^2)$ and $b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2/(\rho_B\rho_A^2)$. Their denominators are at least $(2h/3)^3$, giving the bound in terms of $E$. For any cyclic nonnegative sequence with sum at least $1/2$ and $K<1/8$, every coordinate is at least $1/2$. Otherwise, either all coordinates are below $1/2$, giving $K>\frac14\sum_{i\in[2n]}\widehat u_i\ge1/8$, or a cyclic transition from a coordinate at least $1/2$ to one below $1/2$ contributes more than $1/8$. Using $\widehat u_{i-1}\ge1/2$ in $\widehat u_{i-1}(1-\widehat u_i)^2\le K$ gives $|\widehat u_i-1|\le\sqrt{2K}<1/2$. Thus $h/3<a_i,b_i<3h/2$. Summing and using $S/3<A+B\le S$ yields $S/(9n)<h<3S/(2n)$, which gives the first assertion.

For the second assertion, write $(u_0,u_1,u_2,u_3)\coloneqq(a_i,b_i,a_{i+1},b_{i+1})$ for the consecutive weights of $X_i$. If the last 3 weights are at most $5h/4$, their product with $u_0$ is at most $(125/64)a_i h^3$. Otherwise choose a largest one, say $u_k>5h/4$ for $k\in\{1,2,3\}$. For $k\in\{1,3\}$, the sum $E$ contains $u_{k-1}(u_k-\rho_B)^2$; for $k=2$, it contains $u_1(u_2-\rho_A)^2$. In either case this term is at least $u_{k-1}u_k^2/25$, since $\rho_A,\rho_B\le h<4u_k/5$. If $u_0u_1u_2u_3=0$, the required bound is immediate. Otherwise, the ratio of $u_0u_1u_2u_3$ to $u_{k-1}u_k^2$ is at most $A$. Indeed, for $k=1,2,3$ it is bounded respectively by $u_2,u_0,u_0$. The term $a_i(b_i-\rho_B)^2$ can be used only for $X_{i-1}$ or $X_i$, whereas $b_i(a_{i+1}-\rho_A)^2$ can be used only for $X_i$. Counting each summand of $E$ at most twice therefore gives
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} a_i b_i a_{i+1}b_{i+1}\le50AE+\frac{125}{64}Ah^3
\le\left(50+\frac{125\cdot28}{64}\right)A\Delta
=\frac{1675}{16}A\Delta.\qedhere
\]

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:app-fr-stability}
Let $P$ be a Lagrangian-minimal $r$-palette with $0<\lambda(P)<1$. There are positive integers $k,N$ and a constant $\delta>0$, depending only on $P$, such that every $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$ on $n\ge N$ colors with $d(Q)\ge\lambda(P)-\delta$ admits a complete blowup $S$ of $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ on $C(Q)$ satisfying
\[
d(Q)\le d(S)\le\lambda(P),
\quad\text{and}\quad
|Q\triangle S|\le\frac53\bigl(d(S)-d(Q)\bigr)n^r\le\frac53\bigl(\lambda(P)-d(Q)\bigr)n^r.
\]
Every $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$, regardless of its number of colors or the value of $d(Q)$, satisfies $\lambda(Q)\le\lambda(P)$.
