label: cl:app-fr-minimal
title: Proof
body_md:
Label the colors of $P$ by $[m]$. We first establish rigidity for a fixed finite subpalette of a complete $P$-blowup. Hereditary testability then gives an approximate partition into $m$ parts. Two counting claims compare the tuples violating this partition with the admissible tuples missing from $Q$.

\begin{claim}\label{cl:app-fr-minimal}
The following statements hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Every endomorphism of $P$ is an automorphism, and $P\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$ implies $P\cong\operatorname{rev}(P)$.
\item For each $i\ne j$, there is a tuple in $P$ and a position occupied by $i$ such that replacing that occurrence of $i$ by $j$ gives a tuple outside $P$.
\item There are $\beta,\varepsilon_0>0$ such that $y_i\ge\beta$ for every $i\in[m]$ whenever $\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb{S}_m$ and $\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol y)\ge\lambda(P)-\varepsilon_0$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
For (i), a nonsurjective endomorphism has image $J\subsetneq[m]$. Monotonicity of the Lagrangian under homomorphisms would give $\lambda(P)\le\lambda(P[J])<\lambda(P)$, a contradiction. A bijective endomorphism permutes the finite admissible set and is therefore an automorphism. Since $\Lambda_{\operatorname{rev}(P)[J]}=\Lambda_{P[J]}$, the same argument makes any homomorphism $P\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$ surjective. The two palettes have the same number of admissible tuples, so it is an isomorphism.

For (ii), suppose that replacing any one occurrence of $i$ by $j$ always preserves admissibility. Replacing all occurrences in succession then shows that the map sending $i$ to $j$ and fixing all other colors is an endomorphism. This contradicts (i).

For (iii), minimality implies that every optimal weighting has positive coordinates. By compactness of the set of optimal weightings, choose $\beta>0$ so that every such coordinate exceeds $2\beta$. The maximum of $\Lambda_P$ on the compact set $\{\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb{S}_m\colon\min_{i\in[m]}y_i\le\beta\}$ is then strictly less than $\lambda(P)$. Choosing $\varepsilon_0>0$ smaller than this gap ensures that $\Lambda_P(\boldsymbol y)\ge\lambda(P)-\varepsilon_0$ implies $\min_{i\in[m]}y_i>\beta$, as required.
\end{proof}

Take pairwise disjoint sets $U_1,\ldots,U_m$, each of size $rm$, and let $R_*$ be the rainbow part of the complete $P$-blowup on these parts. We use $R_*$ as the root of the extensions below and write $h\coloneqq |C(R_*)|=rm^2$. Thus a tuple of distinct colors belongs to $R_*$ exactly when the tuple of its part indices belongs to $P$. For $u\in C(R_*)$, a \emph{one-color extension at $u$} retains $R_*$, adds one new color $z$, and adds all tuples obtained by replacing $u$ by $z$ in an admissible tuple of $R_*$. Every added tuple contains $z$ exactly once.

\begin{claim}\label{cl:app-fr-rigidity}
Every homomorphism $\theta\colon R_*\to P$ is constant on each $U_i$, and these constant values define an automorphism of $P$. If $u\in U_i$, then in every homomorphism from the one-color extension at $u$ to $P$, the new color has the same image as $U_i$. If $P\not\cong\operatorname{rev}(P)$, then $R_*\nrightarrow\operatorname{rev}(P)$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
For each $i$, at least $r$ members of $U_i$ have the same image $a_i$. Every admissible tuple of $P$, including one with repeated part indices, can be lifted to distinct representatives among these members. Consequently, $i\mapsto a_i$ is an endomorphism of $P$, and hence an automorphism by \cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(i). Postcomposing $\theta$ with the inverse of this automorphism, assume that $a_i=i$ for all $i$.

Suppose that $u\in U_i$ has image $j\ne i$. Take an arbitrary admissible tuple containing $i$, and lift one occurrence of $i$ to $u$. Lift the other positions to distinct representatives from the subsets of $U_\ell$ whose colors map to $\ell$. Their images show that replacing this occurrence of $i$ by $j$ preserves admissibility. Since the tuple and occurrence were arbitrary, this contradicts \cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(ii). Thus $\theta$ is constant on each $U_i$.

For a one-color extension at $u\in U_i$, postcompose the homomorphism with an automorphism of $P$ so that every color in $U_\ell$ maps to $\ell$ for each $\ell\in[m]$. If the new color has image $j\ne i$, lift any admissible tuple containing $i$ by using $u$ at one chosen occurrence and distinct original colors at the other positions, avoiding $u$. Replace that occurrence of $u$ by the new color. The resulting tuple belongs to the extension and again contradicts \cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(ii). There are enough original colors even when the target tuple repeats $i$, since $|U_i|\ge r$.

Finally, the same choice of representatives applied to a homomorphism $R_*\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$ gives $P\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$. \Cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(i) then gives the last assertion.
\end{proof}

\begin{claim}\label{cl:app-fr-approximation}
For every $\eta>0$, there are positive integers $k_0,N_0$ such that every $Q\in\mathcal C_{k_0}(P)$ on $n\ge N_0$ colors admits a complete blowup $S$ of $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ on $C(Q)$ with $|Q\setminus S|\le\eta n^r$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Delete all tuples of $Q$ with a repeated color, at a cost of at most $\binom r2n^{r-1}$ tuples. Regard the remaining palette as a directed $r$-graph, with its relation defined on ordered tuples of distinct vertices. The property of admitting a homomorphism to $P$ or to $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ is invariant under relabeling and preserved under taking induced subgraphs. Notice that the source tuple has distinct colors, but its image in $P$ may repeat colors.

The testability theorem of Austin and Tao~\cite[Theorem 1.5 in the arXiv version]{austin-tao} supplies $k_0,N_0$ such that, when every restriction to at most $k_0$ vertices has this property, the directed $r$-graph differs in at most $(\eta/2)n^r$ ordered tuples from one that has the property globally. Their edit distance counts unordered $r$-sets on which the induced structure changes; each such set supports at most $r!$ ordered tuples, so tolerance $\eta/2$ gives at most $(\eta/2)r!\binom nr\le(\eta/2)n^r$ ordered-tuple changes.

The defining condition for $\mathcal C_{k_0}(P)$ supplies the required local property. Let $R$ be the modified directed $r$-graph, and let $S$ be the complete blowup defined by a homomorphism from $R$ to $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Since $R\subseteq S$, the rainbow tuples of $Q$ lying outside $S$ are among the edits. Increasing $N_0$ so that $\binom r2n^{r-1}\le(\eta/2)n^r$ proves the claim.
\end{proof}

We now choose the constants for the two counting claims. The root has at most $E\coloneqq h^r$ tuples, so its union with at most $r$ one-color extensions has at most $(r+1)E$ tuples. The constants $c$ and $\gamma$ will be the thresholds in the missing-tuple and degree estimates. Take $\beta,\varepsilon_0$ from \cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(iii), and put $c\coloneqq (\beta/2)^{r-1}/(2(r+1)E)$ and $\gamma\coloneqq c/(4r)$. Put $D_0\coloneqq rm^{r-1}$ and $p_0\coloneqq (\gamma/(4D_0))^m$. Choose $\alpha>0$ so that $\alpha<\varepsilon_0$ and $E\alpha(2/\beta)^r<\min\{p_0/2,1/2\}$. Set $\delta\coloneqq \alpha/4$. Apply \cref{cl:app-fr-approximation} with $\eta=\delta$, and take $k\ge\max\{k_0,h+r\}$. Finally, choose an integer $N\ge\max\{N_0,k\}$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:app-fr-size}
 \beta N\ge2(h+r),\qquad
 r\binom r2\le\frac{\gamma N}{2},\quad\text{and}\quad
 (r-1)h\le\frac{\gamma N}{4D_0}.
\end{equation}

Let $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$ have $n\ge N$ colors and satisfy $d(Q)\ge\lambda(P)-\delta$. \Cref{cl:app-fr-approximation} supplies a complete blowup of $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Replacing $P$ by $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ if necessary, assume that the target of this blowup is $P$. We have $\Lambda_{\operatorname{rev}(P)}=\Lambda_P$, and the preceding constants are unchanged. Among all complete $P$-blowups on $C(Q)$, choose $S$ minimizing $|Q\setminus S|$. Put $B\coloneqq Q\setminus S$ and $A\coloneqq S\setminus Q$, and write the parts of $S$ as $V_1,\ldots,V_m$. Then $|B|\le\delta n^r$ and $|A|=|B|+|S|-|Q|\le2\delta n^r\le\alpha n^r$.
Moreover, we have $d(S)\ge d(Q)-|B|/n^r\ge\lambda(P)-2\delta$. Hence \cref{cl:app-fr-minimal}(iii) gives $|V_i|\ge\beta n$ for every $i\in[m]$.

We will repeatedly choose a uniformly random injective map $\psi\colon C(R_*)\to C(Q)$ with $\psi(U_i)\subseteq V_i$, avoiding a prescribed set of at most $r$ colors. For any fixed ordered tuple of $t\le r$ distinct root colors, the probability of a specified image is at most $(\beta n/2)^{-t}$. Indeed, the denominator is a product of falling factorials, and each factor is at least $\beta n-h-r\ge\beta n/2$. Since $|R_*|\le E$, the probability that some root tuple maps to $A$ is at most
\begin{equation}\label{eq:app-fr-root-failure}
 E|A|\left(\frac{\beta n}{2}\right)^{-r}\le E\alpha\left(\frac{2}{\beta}\right)^r.
\end{equation}

For $x\in C(Q)$, define $d_B(x)\coloneqq|\{(v_1,\ldots,v_r)\in B\colon x\in\{v_1,\ldots,v_r\}\}|$. Thus each tuple is counted once even if $x$ occurs in several positions.

\begin{claim}\label{cl:app-fr-bad-degree}
For every $x\in C(Q)$, we have $d_B(x)\le\gamma n^{r-1}$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Suppose that $d_B(x)>\gamma n^{r-1}$. For each $i\in[m]$, change only the part assigned to $x$, placing it in $V_i$. Let $B_i(x)$ be the tuples of $Q$ containing $x$ that lie outside the resulting blowup. The choice of $S$ gives $|B_i(x)|\ge d_B(x)>\gamma n^{r-1}$. There are at most $r\binom r2n^{r-2}$ tuples containing $x$ and a repeated color. This bound follows by specifying a position occupied by $x$ and a pair of positions with equal entries. By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-size}, at least $(\gamma/2)n^{r-1}$ members of each $B_i(x)$ are rainbow.

For each $i\in[m]$, classify the rainbow tuples in $B_i(x)$ by the position of $x$ and the part indices of the other $r-1$ entries. There are at most $D_0$ types. Hence, for every $i$, choose a set $\mathcal B_i\subseteq B_i(x)$ of one type with $|\mathcal B_i|\ge(\gamma/(2D_0))n^{r-1}$. The corresponding tuple of part indices lies outside $P$ when $x$ is assigned to part $i$. Reserve $r-1$ root colors in the corresponding parts $U_j$ for this type, using disjoint reserved colors for different $i$. There are $(r-1)m$ reserved colors in total, while each $U_j$ has $rm$ colors.

Choose $\psi$ as above, avoiding $x$, and expose these reserved groups in order. Suppose that the previously exposed images form a set $W$. Then $|W|\le h$, and at most $(r-1)|W|n^{r-2}$ members of $\mathcal B_i$ meet $W$. By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-size}, at least $(\gamma/(4D_0))n^{r-1}$ candidates remain. Conditional on the previously exposed images, the current group is uniformly distributed over its permissible ordered images, of which there are at most $n^{r-1}$. Its conditional probability of giving a tuple in $\mathcal B_i$, together with $x$, is therefore at least $\gamma/(4D_0)$. This bound holds for every previous exposure, so all $m$ groups succeed with probability at least $p_0$.

By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-root-failure} and the choice of $\alpha$, the probability that some admissible tuple of $R_*$ is mapped outside $Q$ is less than $p_0/2$. Thus some such injection maps every admissible tuple of $R_*$ into $Q$, and the images of the $m$ reserved groups give tuples in $\mathcal B_1,\ldots,\mathcal B_m$, respectively, when combined with $x$.

Consider the subpalette of $Q$ on $\psi(C(R_*))\cup\{x\}$ consisting of the image of $R_*$ and the $m$ selected tuples from the sets $\mathcal B_i$. It has $h+1\le k$ colors but admits no homomorphism to $P$. Indeed, \cref{cl:app-fr-rigidity} fixes the root labels up to an automorphism. After postcomposing a homomorphism with the inverse of the induced automorphism of $P$, each possible image $i$ of $x$ is excluded by the selected tuple from $\mathcal B_i$. There is no homomorphism to $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ either. If the targets are not isomorphic, the root already excludes such a homomorphism; otherwise, compose it with an isomorphism to $P$. Any homomorphism from the induced palette on these colors would also be a homomorphism from this subpalette. This contradicts $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$.
\end{proof}

We next give a lower bound on the number of missing tuples associated with each $b\in B$. For $b\in B$, let $X$ be the set of colors occurring in $b$, and let $A_1(b)$ consist of the rainbow tuples in $A$ containing exactly 1 color from $X$.

\begin{claim}\label{cl:app-fr-missing}
For every $b\in B$, we have $|A_1(b)|\ge cn^{r-1}$.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
Write $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}$, where $\ell\le r$. For each $j$, choose an original root color in $U_i$ where $x_j\in V_i$, and form its one-color extension with new color $z_j$. Take the union of these extensions with their common root $R_*$. Do not add other tuples containing 2 distinct new colors. Finally, add the tuple obtained from $b$ by replacing every occurrence of $x_j$ by $z_j$.

Call the resulting palette $T_b$. It has at most $h+r\le k$ colors. By \cref{cl:app-fr-rigidity}, any homomorphism $T_b\to P$ can be postcomposed with an automorphism of $P$ so that each $U_i$ maps to $i$; it must then send $z_j$ to the part label of $x_j$. The image of the tuple corresponding to $b$ therefore lies outside $P$, since $b\notin S$. As in the preceding claim, there is no homomorphism to $\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Consequently, there is no injective homomorphism $T_b\to Q$. Indeed, its image $J$ would have at most $k$ colors, so $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$ would give $Q[J]\to P$ or $Q[J]\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Composing with $T_b\to Q[J]$ would contradict the preceding exclusions.

Fix $z_j\mapsto x_j$ and choose a uniformly random injection of the root mapping each $U_i$ into $V_i$, avoiding $X$. The tuple corresponding to $b$ maps to $b\in Q$. Every other tuple of $T_b$ maps into $S$ and is rainbow; its image meets $X$ in 0 or 1 color. Since no such injection is a homomorphism, the image of at least one of these tuples lies outside $Q$. By \eqref{eq:app-fr-root-failure}, with probability greater than $1/2$ every admissible tuple of $R_*$ is mapped into $Q$. Thus with probability at least $1/2$ some tuple of $T_b$ maps to $A_1(b)$.

Besides the tuple corresponding to $b$, $T_b$ has at most $(r+1)E$ tuples. Fix $a\in A_1(b)$ and a tuple of $T_b$ containing one new color. Its new color has a prescribed image, and its other $r-1$ colors are distinct root colors. The probability that its image is $a$ is at most $(\beta n/2)^{-(r-1)}$. A union bound gives $\frac12\le |A_1(b)|(r+1)E(\beta n/2)^{-(r-1)}$, which proves the claim. The construction also applies when $b$ repeats colors, since it uses one new color for each member of $X$, with repeated occurrences using that same new color. All the other added tuples still contain exactly 1 new color.
\end{proof}

By \cref{cl:app-fr-bad-degree,cl:app-fr-missing}, double counting the pairs $(a,b)$ with $b\in B$ and $a\in A_1(b)$ gives
\[
 cn^{r-1}|B|
 \le\sum_{b\in B}|A_1(b)|
 \le r\gamma n^{r-1}|A|.
\]
For the upper bound, each tuple $a\in A$ has at most $r$ colors, and at most $\gamma n^{r-1}$ tuples of $B$ contain any one of them. Thus $|A|\ge4|B|$, so $|S|-|Q|=|A|-|B|\ge0$ and we have
\[
 |Q\triangle S|=|A|+|B|
 \le\frac53(|A|-|B|)
 =\frac53\bigl(d(S)-d(Q)\bigr)n^r.
\]
Since $d(S)\le\lambda(P)$, this proves the stability assertion.

To prove $\lambda(Q)\le\lambda(P)$ for every $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$, suppose instead that some such $Q$ has $\lambda(Q)>\lambda(P)$. Choose a rational probability weighting $\boldsymbol x\in\mathbb{S}_{C(Q)}$ with $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol x)>\lambda(P)$. Complete blowups of $Q$ in these proportions, on arbitrarily many colors, belong to $\mathcal C_k(P)$ and have density $\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol x)$ under the uniform weighting. These blowups satisfy the hypotheses of the density assertion just proved, which bounds their densities by $\lambda(P)$, a contradiction.

For every $x\in C(Q)$, we have $d_B(x)\le\gamma n^{r-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $d_B(x)>\gamma n^{r-1}$. For each $i\in[m]$, change only the part assigned to $x$, placing it in $V_i$. Let $B_i(x)$ be the tuples of $Q$ containing $x$ that lie outside the resulting blowup. The choice of $S$ gives $|B_i(x)|\ge d_B(x)>\gamma n^{r-1}$. There are at most $r\binom r2n^{r-2}$ tuples containing $x$ and a repeated color. This bound follows by specifying a position occupied by $x$ and a pair of positions with equal entries. By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-size}, at least $(\gamma/2)n^{r-1}$ members of each $B_i(x)$ are rainbow.

For each $i\in[m]$, classify the rainbow tuples in $B_i(x)$ by the position of $x$ and the part indices of the other $r-1$ entries. There are at most $D_0$ types. Hence, for every $i$, choose a set $\mathcal B_i\subseteq B_i(x)$ of one type with $|\mathcal B_i|\ge(\gamma/(2D_0))n^{r-1}$. The corresponding tuple of part indices lies outside $P$ when $x$ is assigned to part $i$. Reserve $r-1$ root colors in the corresponding parts $U_j$ for this type, using disjoint reserved colors for different $i$. There are $(r-1)m$ reserved colors in total, while each $U_j$ has $rm$ colors.

Choose $\psi$ as above, avoiding $x$, and expose these reserved groups in order. Suppose that the previously exposed images form a set $W$. Then $|W|\le h$, and at most $(r-1)|W|n^{r-2}$ members of $\mathcal B_i$ meet $W$. By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-size}, at least $(\gamma/(4D_0))n^{r-1}$ candidates remain. Conditional on the previously exposed images, the current group is uniformly distributed over its permissible ordered images, of which there are at most $n^{r-1}$. Its conditional probability of giving a tuple in $\mathcal B_i$, together with $x$, is therefore at least $\gamma/(4D_0)$. This bound holds for every previous exposure, so all $m$ groups succeed with probability at least $p_0$.

By~\eqref{eq:app-fr-root-failure} and the choice of $\alpha$, the probability that some admissible tuple of $R_*$ is mapped outside $Q$ is less than $p_0/2$. Thus some such injection maps every admissible tuple of $R_*$ into $Q$, and the images of the $m$ reserved groups give tuples in $\mathcal B_1,\ldots,\mathcal B_m$, respectively, when combined with $x$.

Consider the subpalette of $Q$ on $\psi(C(R_*))\cup\{x\}$ consisting of the image of $R_*$ and the $m$ selected tuples from the sets $\mathcal B_i$. It has $h+1\le k$ colors but admits no homomorphism to $P$. Indeed, \cref{cl:app-fr-rigidity} fixes the root labels up to an automorphism. After postcomposing a homomorphism with the inverse of the induced automorphism of $P$, each possible image $i$ of $x$ is excluded by the selected tuple from $\mathcal B_i$. There is no homomorphism to $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ either. If the targets are not isomorphic, the root already excludes such a homomorphism; otherwise, compose it with an isomorphism to $P$. Any homomorphism from the induced palette on these colors would also be a homomorphism from this subpalette. This contradicts $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$.

title: Claim
body_md:
\label{cl:app-fr-missing}
For every $b\in B$, we have $|A_1(b)|\ge cn^{r-1}$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_\ell\}$, where $\ell\le r$. For each $j$, choose an original root color in $U_i$ where $x_j\in V_i$, and form its one-color extension with new color $z_j$. Take the union of these extensions with their common root $R_*$. Do not add other tuples containing 2 distinct new colors. Finally, add the tuple obtained from $b$ by replacing every occurrence of $x_j$ by $z_j$.

Call the resulting palette $T_b$. It has at most $h+r\le k$ colors. By \cref{cl:app-fr-rigidity}, any homomorphism $T_b\to P$ can be postcomposed with an automorphism of $P$ so that each $U_i$ maps to $i$; it must then send $z_j$ to the part label of $x_j$. The image of the tuple corresponding to $b$ therefore lies outside $P$, since $b\notin S$. As in the preceding claim, there is no homomorphism to $\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Consequently, there is no injective homomorphism $T_b\to Q$. Indeed, its image $J$ would have at most $k$ colors, so $Q\in\mathcal C_k(P)$ would give $Q[J]\to P$ or $Q[J]\to\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Composing with $T_b\to Q[J]$ would contradict the preceding exclusions.

Fix $z_j\mapsto x_j$ and choose a uniformly random injection of the root mapping each $U_i$ into $V_i$, avoiding $X$. The tuple corresponding to $b$ maps to $b\in Q$. Every other tuple of $T_b$ maps into $S$ and is rainbow; its image meets $X$ in 0 or 1 color. Since no such injection is a homomorphism, the image of at least one of these tuples lies outside $Q$. By \eqref{eq:app-fr-root-failure}, with probability greater than $1/2$ every admissible tuple of $R_*$ is mapped into $Q$. Thus with probability at least $1/2$ some tuple of $T_b$ maps to $A_1(b)$.

Besides the tuple corresponding to $b$, $T_b$ has at most $(r+1)E$ tuples. Fix $a\in A_1(b)$ and a tuple of $T_b$ containing one new color. Its new color has a prescribed image, and its other $r-1$ colors are distinct root colors. The probability that its image is $a$ is at most $(\beta n/2)^{-(r-1)}$. A union bound gives $\frac12\le |A_1(b)|(r+1)E(\beta n/2)^{-(r-1)}$, which proves the claim. The construction also applies when $b$ repeats colors, since it uses one new color for each member of $X$, with repeated occurrences using that same new color. All the other added tuples still contain exactly 1 new color.

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), approximate $\boldsymbol x$ by rational weightings $\boldsymbol x^{(j)}$, and take complete $Q$-blowups $Q_j$ in these proportions, with $n_j\coloneqq |C(Q_j)|$ chosen so that $\lim_{j\to\infty}n_j=\infty$. They belong to $\mathcal C_k(P)$ and satisfy $d(Q_j)=\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol x^{(j)})$, so $\lim_{j\to\infty}d(Q_j)=\Lambda_Q(\boldsymbol x)$. For all sufficiently large $j$, we may therefore apply \cref{prop:app-fr-stability} and let $S_j$ be the resulting complete blowup of $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Pass to a subsequence with a fixed target $P'$. If the parts of $S_j$ are $V_1^{(j)},\ldots,V_m^{(j)}$, put $z_{v,i}^{(j)}\coloneqq|\{u\in V_i^{(j)}\colon u\text{ is a clone of }v\}|/n_j$ for $v\in C(Q)$ and $i\in[m]$. Pass to a convergent subsequence of this finite-dimensional array. Its limit satisfies $\sum_{i=1}^m z_{v,i}=\lim_{j\to\infty}\sum_{i=1}^m z_{v,i}^{(j)}=\lim_{j\to\infty}x_v^{(j)}=x_v$ for every $v\in C(Q)$.

At $\boldsymbol z^{(j)}$, the left side of~\eqref{eq:app-fr-split} is exactly $|Q_j\triangle S_j|/n_j^r$. Indeed, for fixed $\boldsymbol v,\boldsymbol i$, the number of ordered tuples of colors in $Q_j$ whose $a$th entry is a clone of $v_a$ in $V_{i_a}^{(j)}$ for every $a\in[r]$ is $\prod_{a\in[r]}(n_jz_{v_a,i_a}^{(j)})$. This count also holds when entries repeat, since the same color of $Q_j$ may occupy more than one position. Passing to the limit in the estimate from~\cref{prop:app-fr-stability} proves the result.

For (ii), apply (i). The right side of \eqref{eq:app-fr-split} is zero. For every $v\in J$, choose a label $\phi(v)$ with $z_{v,\phi(v)}>0$. For each $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)\in J^r$, including tuples with repeated colors, we have $\prod_{a\in[r]}z_{v_a,\phi(v_a)}>0$. All summands in~\eqref{eq:app-fr-split} are nonnegative, so $(v_1,\ldots,v_r)\in Q\Longleftrightarrow(\phi(v_1),\ldots,\phi(v_r))\in P'$. Thus $Q[J]$ is a complete blowup of $P'$. Since $J$ supports an optimal weighting of $Q$, we have $\lambda(Q[J])=\lambda(Q)=\lambda(P)$. The map $\phi$ is therefore surjective. Otherwise, monotonicity of the Lagrangian under homomorphisms and minimality would give $\lambda(Q[J])\le\lambda(P'[\phi(J)])<\lambda(P)$.

If, in addition, $\boldsymbol x$ has minimum support, no part can contain two positive-weight colors. Indeed, the polynomial of a complete blowup depends only on the total weight in each part, so concentrating that weight on one color preserves the polynomial value and reduces the size of the support. Thus each part contains exactly 1 positive-weight color, proving the minimum-support assertion in (ii).

For (iii), choose an optimal weighting $\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb{S}_m$ of $P$. For each $n$, choose nonnegative integers $n_1,\ldots,n_m$ summing to $n$ with $|n_i/n-y_i|\le1/n$ for every $i\in[m]$. The vector $(n_i/n)_{i\in[m]}$ differs from $\boldsymbol y$ by at most $m/n$ in the $\ell^1$ norm. The difference-of-products bound in the proof of \cref{thm:compactness} therefore gives $\Lambda_P((n_i/n)_{i\in[m]})\ge\lambda(P)-rm/n$. This is the density of the complete $P$-blowup with part sizes $n_1,\ldots,n_m$. All complete blowups of $P$ or $\operatorname{rev}(P)$ are $\mathcal G$-deficient. A $\mathcal G$-deficient palette $Q$ with the maximum number of tuples therefore belongs to $\mathcal C_k(P)$ and satisfies the density hypothesis of \cref{prop:app-fr-stability} for sufficiently large $n$. Let $S$ be the complete blowup supplied by that proposition. Since $S$ is also $\mathcal G$-deficient, the choice of $Q$ gives $d(Q)\ge d(S)$. The two inequalities in \cref{prop:app-fr-stability} imply $d(Q)=d(S)$ and $Q=S$.

label: prop:countable-colorability
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), write $x_{ij}$ for the weight of the color $\{i,j\}$. Since each triangle gives 6 admissible tuples, the polynomial of $P_m$ is
\[
\Lambda_{P_m}(\boldsymbol x)=6\sum_{1\le i<j<k\le m}x_{ij}x_{ik}x_{jk}.
\]
Assigning weight $1/3$ to each edge of one triangle gives $\lambda(P_m)\ge2/9$. For the reverse bound, choose an optimal probability weighting with minimum support. If 2 disjoint edges have positive weight, no triangle contains both, so the polynomial is affine when weight is transferred between them. Concentrating their total weight on one of the 2 edges cannot decrease the value and reduces the support, a contradiction. Thus the edges of positive weight are pairwise intersecting. Since the polynomial value is positive, they contain a triangle. Any other edge is disjoint from at least one edge of this triangle, so the support consists of exactly its 3 edges. AM--GM therefore gives $\lambda(P_m)\le6(1/3)^3=2/9$. Every finite subset of $C(P)$ is contained in $\binom{[m]}2$ for some $m$, so the definition of the countable-palette Lagrangian gives $\lambda(P)=\sup_{m\ge3}\lambda(P_m)=2/9$.

For (ii), label the vertices of a finite $3$-graph by $[n]$ and color each pair by itself, that is, $\chi(\{i,j\})\coloneqq\{i,j\}$. For every edge $\{i<j<k\}$, the face colors in the prescribed order are $(\{j,k\},\{i,k\},\{i,j\})$, which form an admissible tuple of $P$. Hence every finite $3$-graph is $P$-colorable.

In contrast, for a fixed $m\ge3$, Ramsey's theorem~\cite[Theorem B]{ramsey} implies that every coloring of the pairs of a sufficiently large vertex set with the $\binom m2$ colors of $P_m$ contains a monochromatic triangle. Its 3 face colors form a tuple $(e,e,e)$, which is not admissible in $P_m$. Thus no vertex order and pair coloring can make the complete $3$-graph on this vertex set $P_m$-colorable.

label: lem:order-amplification
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:order-amplification}
Let $r\ge3$, let $R$ be a finite $r$-palette, and let $\mathscr T$ be any collection of $r$-palettes. Suppose there are finite ordered $r$-graphs $H^+,H^-$, each containing an edge, that are $R$-colorable, such that $H^+$ is not $T$-colorable and $H^-$ is not $\operatorname{rev}(T)$-colorable for any $T\in\mathscr T$. Then there is a finite unordered $r$-graph $G\in\operatorname{Col}(R)$ that does not belong to $\operatorname{Col}(T)$ for any $T\in\mathscr T$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Add isolated vertices so that both ordered $r$-graphs have $v$ vertices, and put $m\coloneqq(v-1)^2+1$. For sufficiently large $N$, a greedy packing gives at least $\eta_mN^2$ subsets of $[N]$, each of size $m$, any two meeting in at most 1 vertex, where $\eta_m>0$ depends only on $m$. Indeed, each selected $m$-set rules out at most $\binom m2\binom{N-2}{m-2}$ candidates, out of $\binom Nm$ in total.

Independently color every $(r-1)$-set of $[N]$ uniformly from $C(R)$, and retain every $r$-set whose tuple in the natural order belongs to $R$. The resulting unordered $r$-graph is $R$-colorable.

Fix an order $\prec$ of $[N]$. In each packed $m$-set, the monotone-subsequence theorem~\cite[p.~467]{erdosszekeres} gives $v$ vertices whose natural order agrees with $\prec$ or reverses it. Choose this subset deterministically from the two orders. Fix an $R$-coloring of each witness, extending it arbitrarily to faces outside its edges. On the chosen vertices in their natural order, require the fixed coloring of $H^+$ in the agreeing case and that of $H^-$ in the reversing case. Each prescribed coloring occurs with probability $p\coloneqq|C(R)|^{-\binom v{r-1}}>0$. On the corresponding event, the selected vertices contain $H^+$ or $H^-$, respectively, in the natural order. In order $\prec$, the latter is $(H^-)^{\rm rev}$, which cannot be $T$-colored because $H^-$ cannot be $\operatorname{rev}(T)$-colored. Either event therefore excludes every $T\in\mathscr T$ at once.

The events for distinct packed sets use disjoint $(r-1)$-faces because $r-1\ge2$, so they are independent. The failure probability for this order is at most $(1-p)^{\eta_mN^2}$. Taking a union bound over all $N!$ orders gives total failure probability at most $N!(1-p)^{\eta_mN^2}<1$ for sufficiently large $N$. Some resulting $r$-graph therefore excludes every target palette in every vertex order.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $a=0$ or $b=0$, both conclusions give zero. Assume that $a,b>0$. For a $(k+s)$-palette $R$ and $\varnothing\ne I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_t\}\subseteq[k+s]$, its \emph{coordinate projection} is the $t$-palette $R_I\coloneqq\{(c_{i_1},\ldots,c_{i_t})\colon(c_1,\ldots,c_{k+s})\in R\}$ on $C(R)$. Each projected tuple is included only once. We first check how a coloring of a coordinate projection extends after common vertices are added to every edge.

\begin{claim}\label{clm:cone-projection}
Let $R$ be a finite $(k+s)$-palette, and let $R_I$ be its projection onto the first $k$ coordinates. If an ordered $k$-graph $F$ is $R_I$-colorable, then the ordered $(k+s)$-graph obtained by adding the same $s$ new vertices to every edge, placing all new vertices last, is $R$-colorable. The analogous statement holds for the last $s$ coordinates by placing $k$ new vertices first.
\end{claim}
\begin{proof}[Proof of the claim]
For each edge $e$ of $F$, choose an admissible $R$-tuple completing its prescribed projected tuple. If $Z$ is the set of new vertices, the faces $(e\setminus\{v\})\cup Z$ use the original face colors. They agree whenever shared by different edges. The other faces are $e\cup(Z\setminus\{z\})$. Such a face determines both $e$ and $z$, since the old and new vertex sets are disjoint, so its completion color can be chosen independently for each edge. This gives a consistent coloring. Similarly, for projection onto the last $s$ coordinates, place the new vertices first.
\end{proof}

Choose forbidden families $\mathcal F,\mathcal G$ with densities $a,b$. By~\cref{thm:palette-tools}(i), the finite $\mathcal F$-deficient palettes have Lagrangians with supremum $a$, and the finite $\mathcal G$-deficient palettes have Lagrangians with supremum $b$. Both deficiency conditions are preserved when palettes are reversed.

We first prove that $ab\in\Pi_{\mathrm u,\infty}^{(k+s)}$. Let $\mathscr T_\diamond$ consist of all products $P\diamond Q$ with $P$ a finite $\mathcal F$-deficient palette and $Q$ a finite $\mathcal G$-deficient palette. Its Lagrangians have supremum $ab$. For every finite $(k+s)$-palette $R$ with $\lambda(R)>ab$, we will construct a finite $(k+s)$-graph that is $R$-colorable but is not colorable by any member of $\mathscr T_\diamond$.

Put $I\coloneqq[k]$ and $J\coloneqq[k+s]\setminus I$, and let $R_I,R_J$ be the projections of $R$ onto these position sets. For every probability weighting $\boldsymbol x$ on $C(R)$, we have $\Lambda_R(\boldsymbol x)\le\Lambda_{R_I}(\boldsymbol x)\Lambda_{R_J}(\boldsymbol x)$.
The pointwise inequality follows by expanding the product, since every tuple in $R$ contributes one of its terms. Taking maxima gives $\lambda(R)\le\lambda(R_I)\lambda(R_J)$. Hence $\lambda(R_I)>a$ or $\lambda(R_J)>b$. In the first case some $F\in\mathcal F$ is $R_I$-colorable. Choose a witnessing order and apply \cref{clm:cone-projection}. The resulting ordered $(k+s)$-graph is $R$-colorable but cannot be colored by any $P\diamond Q\in\mathscr T_\diamond$. Indeed, such a coloring would induce a $P$-coloring of $F$ by taking the first component of each color on the faces in the first coordinate block. The second case uses a member of $\mathcal G$ and places the new vertices first.

We also need a witness against all reversed targets. Interchanging the components of each color gives $\operatorname{rev}(P\diamond Q)\cong\operatorname{rev}(Q)\diamond\operatorname{rev}(P)$. Apply the same argument with the blocks of sizes $s,k$ and the deficiency classes interchanged. The threshold remains $ab$, so it supplies another ordered $R$-colorable witness excluding every reversed target. \Cref{lem:order-amplification} gives a finite unordered $(k+s)$-graph $G_R$ that is $R$-colorable and is not colorable by any member of $\mathscr T_\diamond$.

Let $\mathcal H_\diamond$ consist of one such $G_R$ for every finite palette $R$ with $\lambda(R)>ab$, taking representatives on finite labeled color sets. Every target product is deficient for this family, so~\cref{thm:palette-tools}(i) gives density at least $ab$. Every palette with larger Lagrangian colors its designated $G_R$, giving the reverse bound. Hence $\pi_{k+s-2}(\mathcal H_\diamond)=ab$.

For the product on disjoint color sets, consider the products $P\star Q$ of a finite $\mathcal F$-deficient palette $P$ and a finite $\mathcal G$-deficient palette $Q$. Their Lagrangians have supremum $\frac{k^ks^sab}{(k+s)^{k+s}}$. Fix a finite $(k+s)$-palette $R$ with larger Lagrangian, and put $C_I\coloneqq\{c_i\colon(c_1,\ldots,c_{k+s})\in R,\ i\in I\}$ and $C_J\coloneqq\{c_j\colon(c_1,\ldots,c_{k+s})\in R,\ j\in J\}$, the sets of colors occurring in the two coordinate blocks. We construct the ordered witness in two cases.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Suppose $C_I\cap C_J\ne\varnothing$. Choose tuples in which a common color occurs at positions $p\in I$ and $q\in J$. The ordered edges $[k+s+1]\setminus\{p\}$ and $[k+s+1]\setminus\{q+1\}$ share a face at positions $q$ and $p$, respectively. Assign to the first edge the tuple with the common color at position $q$, and to the second the tuple with that color at position $p$. Every other face belongs to just one edge, so the assignment gives an $R$-coloring. No $P\star Q$ colors this ordered $(k+s)$-graph, because its two coordinate blocks use disjoint color sets.
\item Suppose $C_I\cap C_J=\varnothing$. After deleting unused colors, $R_I$ and $R_J$ have disjoint color sets $C_I$ and $C_J$, and $R$ is a subpalette of $R_I\star R_J$. These deletions preserve all three Lagrangians, so \cref{lem:finite-products} gives $\lambda(R)\le\frac{k^ks^s}{(k+s)^{k+s}}\lambda(R_I)\lambda(R_J)$. Thus $\lambda(R_I)>a$ or $\lambda(R_J)>b$. In the first case, choose an $R_I$-colorable $F\in\mathcal F$ and apply \cref{clm:cone-projection} to a witnessing order. The resulting ordered $(k+s)$-graph is $R$-colorable but cannot be colored by any of the products $P\star Q$, since projection onto the first $k$ positions would give a $P$-coloring of $F$. In the second case, use an $R_J$-colorable member of $\mathcal G$ and place the new vertices first; projection onto the last $s$ positions gives the analogous contradiction.
\end{enumerate}
Finally, we have
$\operatorname{rev}(P\star Q)=\operatorname{rev}(Q)\star\operatorname{rev}(P)$ after relabeling the disjoint color sets, so the same construction works for the reversed targets. Apply \cref{lem:order-amplification} to obtain an unordered $R$-colorable witness excluding every product $P\star Q$ under consideration. Form a forbidden family from one such witness for each finite $(k+s)$-palette $R$ with $\lambda(R)>\frac{k^ks^sab}{(k+s)^{k+s}}$. By~\cref{thm:palette-tools}(i), this family has density $\frac{k^ks^sab}{(k+s)^{k+s}}$.

title: Proof
body_md: Choose $N$ with $\lambda(P_N)<4r^{-r}$, so $P_N$ is rainbow. For $n\ge N$, composition gives a homomorphism $\theta_n\colon P_n\to P_N$. For each $c\in C(P_N)$, every admissible tuple of $P_n$ has at most 1 entry in $\theta_n^{-1}(c)$, so $\Lambda_{P_n}$ is affine in the weights within this set when all other weights are fixed. Starting from an optimal weighting, successively concentrate the total weight of each nonempty set $\theta_n^{-1}(c)$ on 1 color without decreasing the polynomial. Thus $\lambda(P_n)$ is attained on at most $|C(P_N)|$ colors. Only finitely many palette Lagrangians occur on that many colors. Since $(\lambda(P_n))_{n\ge N}$ is nonincreasing with limit $t$, increasing $N$ if necessary gives $\lambda(P_n)=t$ for every $n\ge N$.
